Giffard Memorial Hospital (GMH), situated in the Nuzvid, Krishna District, Andhra Pradesh, India, is 250-bed general hospital operated by the Medical Educational Trust Association Surat for the General Conference of Seventh-day Adventists, Southern Asia Division.

Since it is in a rural setting, the majority of the patients are peasants and daily wage earners, and the hospital has been registered with the government as a charitable institution. The hospital operates the following departments: general medicine, orthopedics, gynecology, pediatrics, anesthesiology, general surgery, and ophthalmology. The hospital also has a good clinical laboratory, with X-ray, E.C.G., ultrasound scan, and gastroscopy. The institution has a neonatal intensive care unit and also provides chaplaincy services. About 80 churches have been established around Nuzvid as a result of the ministry of GMH.

### Background

The British bestowed titles such as “raja/maharaja” on wealthy _zamindars_ (feudal landlords) who cooperated with them. The titles were hereditary, and their sons were _kumars_ (princes). About 400 years ago, an Indian prince with his retainers had gone out hunting. According to the story, a large hare, instead of fleeing, charged the royal hunting dogs with such fury that they turned tail and ran away in fright. The prince’s advisors told him that this was proof that this land was extremely fertile, and they counseled him to move his palace and fort to this site. This prince built a town and named it Nu-ja-veedu (Nuzvid), recalling the incident in the _nuvulu_ (sesame) field.1

In the early 20th century, a _zamindar_ (the Rajah of Teleprole) emulated his father who had vowed to alleviate the sufferings of the poorer classes. At the palace gates, he dispensed medicines for common ailments, but lamented his inability to help in maternity cases. To further fulfill his father’s vow and to memorialize his father, he started building a hospital investing 30,000 dollars. Impressed, the local British government also decided to assist financially. In 1912, Colonel Giffard of the Government Maternity Hospital in Madras laid the foundation stone of the hospital. Because of the World War I and related difficulties, the government was unable to assist, and the buildings were left incomplete.

In 1922, an Adventist missionary named Theodore Flaiz set out for Vijaywada to do some ingathering. A suspended employee of the church who was trying to regain favor hitched a ride with him and persuaded Flaiz to visit his “friend,” the raja at Nuzvid, where the missionary would be assured of success. Flaiz complied. While the Raja disowned any knowledge of his companion (who had stayed back), upon hearing of the plans to help the poor in the community, he offered the missionary five acres of land and the unfinished buildings of the hospital plus Rs 10,000 to complete them. The only condition was that the hospital should be named in honor of his friend Colonel Giffard, who had laid the foundation stone ten years earlier.2

### Establishing the Hospital

The hospital was named Giffard Mission Hospital. An agreement was signed between Shree Rajah Sobhanadri Apparao, _zamindar_ of Telaprole, and the India Financial Association of Seventh-day Adventists that detailed the transfer of assets and continuing obligations of both parties.3 The cook house and servants’ quarters were practically complete, but the three wards were only completed up to the wall plates.4

In answer to a call for a physician, the Mission Board sent Dr. Arthur E. Coyne from Loma Linda University. After some post-graduate study in England on the way5 and a year of language study, he opened Giffard Mission Hospital on September 15, 1925.6 Dr. Coyne had not planned to begin so early as the buildings were not yet complete, but patients had started coming so the doctor began to treat them.7 At the time of opening, the staff of twelve included a midwife, a compounder (pharmacist), two dressers, three attendants, two gardeners, a caretaker, a laundryman, and a sweeper. The bed capacity was 21.8

A few years later, the raja donated another Rs 10,000 to complete the nurses’ quarters and to construct a compound wall to keep out the cattle. 9 Whereas the perception of some was that Adventist sanitariums tended to cater to the wealthy in the big cities, this one served the poor in the villages.10

When Mrs. Coyne remarked that a church would be needed, the zamindar responded that he had already realized that two years earlier and had purchased a plot of land opposite the hospital. He had the church constructed there.11

### Early Developments

In the early years, zamindars helped to provide funds for new additions including a beautiful, up-to-date operating room, a reading room, guestroom, and private cottages. The Zamindar of Telaprole was active in promoting the growth of the hospital.

On March 3, 1936, a new ward was opened that was built of stone from the zamindar’s own quarries. The ward was roofed with Mangalore tile. A wide veranda ran nearly around the entire ward. On either side of the broad steps were ramps for stretchers and wheelchairs. The spacious ward contained eight modern hospital beds. The galvanized-iron ceiling was painted a restful light green. The rows of immaculate white beds, done up with new linen, made an inviting scene. At one end of the main ward were two private rooms for patients, and at the other end was a nursery with six little cribs. Behind the ward, connected by porches, was a building with the bathrooms.12

The first x-ray machine was brought by Dr. Douglas W. Semmens when he returned from furlough. This was a gift to the Giffard Mission Hospital from medical friends in America. Dr. Elizabeth J. Hiscox, who was associated with Doctor Semmens was experienced in X-ray work and took charge of this new department.13

Five years after the donation, more than 300 villages were represented by the patients who came to the hospital during one month. The average number of those ministered to in one way or another by the institution was more than 2,000 patients a month.14

### World War II

From 1942 to 1944, all the overseas personnel left and, in their absence, the hospital operated as a dispensary managed by B. S. Solomon, Y. Daniel, S. Joseph, and A. Grace. The hospital was reopened for regular work in August 1944 by Dr. Elizabeth J. Hiscox, who had first come to Nuzvid in 1938 but had left in 1942 due to the World War.

T. R. Flaiz, who had negotiated the acquisition of the hospital property and building, had qualified himself as a physician at Loma Linda in 1937, and after working there as vice president for two years and in private practice for another four years, he accepted a call to return to Southern Asia, serving as medical superintendent of GMH and as medical secretary of the Southern Asia Division from 1945-1947.15 During this time, more land was acquired, bed capacity was increased to 108, and the government recognized nurses training school was established.16 He left to serve the General Conference as medical secretary.

During the war years, a group of Seventh-day Adventist medical personnel in the American army were stationed at Ramgarh, 46 km. from Ranchi, the present capital of Jharkhand. They came to Ranchi every Sabbath for church services. Among them was a tall young doctor by the name of John B. Oliver. He was told of the need for doctors in India, and Nuzvid in particular. At the end of the contract with the army, he returned to India with his wife to become the medical superintendent, replacing Dr. Flaiz six months before independence in 1947. He left in 1952, but returned again and again to serve the hospital. During his time, the large Nuzvid SDA auditorium was built.17

During the end portion of the war years, the completed building projects on the compound are as follows: (1) The Flaiz Ward —a new women’s ward named after Dr. T. R. Flaiz, who very competently engineered its construction. It was formally opened on the 23rd of December, 1946; (2) The extension to the surgery — a much-needed building to fall in line with the ever-increasing patronage of the hospital; (3) Kasturi Bai Hall — the library hall that was used by students and workers; (4) a choultry (a resting place) for Christians who were not allowed to stay in the Hindu choultry in town. It consisted of two rooms and a large hall. This was much used great by our church members and workers who came for medical attention and also by Christians of other denominations; and (5) four new workers' cottages in the Garden Compound. As a training school for nurses, the hospital received workers and students from all over the Division and it was to meet that need that those cottages were built.18

Dr. Bazliel, a good orthopedic surgeon, was in charge of the women’s clinic and ward, and Dr. Thomas was in charge of the men’s clinic and ward. Both kept the hospital open in the very hot summer months for the first time. Dr. (Mrs.) Bazliel took care of the women’s clinic for a short time. With all the workers and the European staff back at the close of the War, the hospital once again functioned at full speed. An outpatient clinic was opened on August 5, 1947, in Eluru at the office of Dr. T. John, a former hospital worker. Dr. Oliver, Mr. Eswar Rao, and Miss Janobi opened the clinic. The hospital was engaged in missionary work in conjunction with medical work. Workers took a lively interest in evangelistic endeavors, and branch Sabbath schools were conducted regularly.19

### Maternity Ward

On Sunday December 18, 1955, Shri Bezwada Gopala Reddy, chief minister of Andhra State, opened a new maternity building. Named the “Flaiz Ward” in honor of Dr. Flaiz, who was instrumental in the establishment of the hospital. The ward was donated by the Zamindar of Ellamarru, in memory of his wife. The zamindar’s son was also present as well as about 700 guests. Dr. J. B. Oliver gave a brief history of the hospital and the maternity building, which was followed by the main address given by Shri Bezwada Gopala Reddy.

The new building had 12 beds, one semi-private room, and five private rooms. There was a delivery room, two labor rooms, and nurses’ work rooms. The nursery had large windows on one side, which made it convenient for patients and relatives to see the babies as they were cared for. The donation by the zemindar of Ellamarru was largely responsible for the building while substantial amounts came from Dr. T. R. Flaiz and from the Medical Extension offering.20

### Community Service

At the beginning of 1979, Giffard Memorial Hospital launched a community eye project with Dr. Ronnie Gyi, who held a diploma in ophthalmology, leading the project. With financial backing from the Christophel Blinden Mission, the project was off to a good start. Eight months of groundwork acquainting the surrounding villages of the program paid off with more than 1,000 people screened in one month and 100 cataract surgeries performed. After that, 20 cataract operations were scheduled each week. The CBM continued sponsorship on a large scale.21

### The Golden Jubilee

The people in Nuzvid and around Krishna District and the staff of Giffard Memorial Hospital celebrated the Golden Jubilee on November 11, 1975. Inaugurating the celebrations, M. R. Appa Rao, vice-chancellor of Andhra University, who incidentally was a native of Nuzvid and had taken a keen interest in the development of the hospital, delivered glowing tributes to the dedicated medical work rendered by the hospital through the previous five decades. He made a special mention of Dr. E. J. Hiscox, the female doctor who served the hospital for three decades, comparing her with Mother Theresa of Calcutta in her service for the sick. He recalled how Miss Hiscox pooled all her earnings for several years and donated that amount to build a 50-bed children's ward in the hospital. The ward was inaugurated at that celebration. Mr. Appa Rao further asserted that “service” was the motto of the staff and workers of the Giffard Hospital and it was “written all over the place.” He expressed thanks to those rajahs, whose donations of lands and funds and the incessant care and service of the missionary personages of the SDA Church took to make the medical institution grow to that stature. Mr. Paladugu Venkat Rao, MLC, stated that it was heartening to note that while the medical profession had become a business proposition, such good work was being done at Nuzvid. Presenting a report, Dr. M. Jagannadha Rao, medical director of the hospital, traced the history of the hospital’s development. He paid tributes to the late rajah of Telaprolu, Col. Giffard, the surgeon general of Madras, T. R. Flaiz, who was instrumental in building the hospital and who served for 40 years, and others who helped the hospital to grow. Elder F. W. Wernick, vice president of the General Conference, and Dr. Ost, lay field secretary of the General Conference were specially flown in to participate in the function. Dr. Ost presented awards to the active and retired staff of the hospital. A portrait of the Rajah of Telaprolu was installed at the hospital in the presence of his wife.22

### Pioneering Health Education

The first and only graduates of a two-year theological seminary course at Ibrahimpatnam, about 50 kms from Nuzvid, were also the first to receive health education to prepare them for practical health evangelism. The seminarians spent two months at Nuzvid taking courses in religion and health from a former hospital chaplain and his wife, pastor, and Mrs. Anandaraj and former chaplain and his wife. Medical Director Dr. Philip Viruthan held a graduation service for the trained health evangelists in August 1978. Three graduates were placed in separate villages and were successful in alleviating suffering in those villages. They were much appreciated by the village panchayat and the village residents. In January 1980, the Christian Medical Association of India negotiated funds from a Dutch agency to expand the project. 23

### First Heart Surgery

On March 18, 1982, the hospital conducted its first open heart surgery. With that surgery, Giffard Memorial Hospital provided an effective answer to a narrowed mitral valve—the commonest heart disease seen in India at that time. Despite minor setbacks, the surgery was successful. This was the first Christian-operated heart surgery in the whole state and the first in a rural setting. In the afternoon, a 14-year-old boy with a patent ductus arteriosus, a congenital heart defect, was operated on. The boy had a stormy operative and postoperative period, demanding the best efforts of the chief surgeon, the chief anaesthetic, and chief ICCU nurse, the maintenance and servicing engineer, and a host of others. Both patients became living testimonies to what dedicated and committed service could do despite hardships and handicaps.24

### Management History

When it was established, the hospital was managed by a committee chaired by the superintendent/president of the South India Union. When the hospital reopened in 1945 and and with the establishment of the government nurses training school in 1946, the institution was brought directly under the Division and was managed by a board chaired by the president of the Division.

In the month of February 1998, the Southern Asia Division made changes in the administrative structure of the hospital. Mr. Joshi Victor Rayavarapu was appointed hospital administrator.25 The hospital was modernized and inaugurated by Pastor. D. R. Watts, Division president, on December 6, 1998.

In 2000, the hospital came under the umbrella of the Adventist Health India System, and the board was chaired by the secretary of the AHI.

The Medical Educational Trust Association Surat (METAS) of Seventh-day Adventists took over the operation of the hospital in 2007, with Dr. M.S. Jeremiah as the president & CEO. Since the hospital, school, and college came under one umbrella, executive vice presidents were appointed to assist the president & CEO in managing the administrative affairs.

### College of Nursing

From the time the hospital was first established, Mrs. Coyne, and later Dr. Emma Hughes, taught a few workers some practical nursing. In 1928, the hospital offered a three-year nursing course and a two-year compounder (pharmacy) course. The prerequisite for both was completion of the eighth standard (approximately junior high school). In 1934, the school of nursing was affiliated with the Christian Medical Association of India (CMAI). In 1942, due to World War II, the hospital and the school closed. T. R. Flaiz arrived in India (1945) and revived the nursing program. The first government recognized higher-grade nursing certificate course began in 1946. Government recognition by the Madras Nurse and Midwives Council was granted in 1947 but made retroactive to 1946.26

Needing 200 cases per year in order to begin the midwifery school, Mary Mathews, with a few students, went to the villages constantly seeking expectant mothers. They visited with them, monitored their blood pressures, checked them for anaemia, followed up on their diets and, in some cases, cooked meals for them. They also taught them better dietary habits. The mothers were encouraged to listen to the babies’ heartbeats, which they had never done before. Gradually a few came to the hospital because their nurse friends were there. Infant mortality decreased noticeably in the surrounding villages.27

A one-year matriculate-level course in lab technology and a midwifery course for nurses began in 1952. The lab course was upgraded in 1974 and became a two-year course in 1990. The nursing council integrated the six-month midwifery course into a three-year A-grade nursing course in 1988. 28 The lab school closed in 2009.

At the end of 2006, the Division took an action to transfer management of GMH to the Medical Educational Trust Association, Surat of Seventh-day Adventist METAS for the purpose of developing the nursing school into a college and improving the hospital facilities.29 METAS assumed management of the entire campus, consisting of the high school, the hospital, and the nursing school. The whole area of five acres was cleared and two blocks built for the school of nursing and a college of nursing. The college is affiliated with the Dr. N.T.R. University of Health Sciences, Vijaywada, and offers a four-year B.Sc. Nursing degree.

### Recent Developments

Dr. Eliah Srikakolli, who succeeded Dr. M.S. Jeremiah in 2014, took interest in further developing GMH. In the last few years, a Neonatal Intensive Care Unit became an added asset with the outstanding services of Dr. Edwin Raj, chief medical officer and pediatrician. More comfortable quarters to accommodate doctors were built through the financial contributions of Mrs. Kollabathula Mary Samuel’s children, Dr. Ferdinand Samuel, Mrs. Dorothy Pandit, Mrs. Cathy Samuel, Dr. Vincent Samuel, and their families. These were inaugurated during the COVID pandemic virtually by Elder Ezras Lakra, president of Southern Asia Division. This complex with two floors is named, “Oliver Home,” in honor of Dr. J. B. Oliver. Concrete cement roads were laid in 2020. A state-of-the-art Intensive Care Unit and an additional Neonatal Intensive Care Unit have been constructed.30

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

The **history of hospitals** began in antiquity with [hospitals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hospital "Hospital") in Greece, the Roman Empire, [Sasanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sasanian_Empire "Sasanian Empire")[Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran") and on the Indian subcontinent as well, starting with precursors in the [Asclepian temples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asclepeion "Asclepeion") in [ancient Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greece "Ancient Greece") and then the [military hospitals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicine_in_ancient_Rome#Hospitals "Medicine in ancient Rome") in [ancient Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome"). The Greek temples were dedicated to the sick and infirm but did not look anything like modern hospitals. The Romans did not have dedicated, public hospitals. Public hospitals, per se, did not exist until the Christian period.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-clean-1) Towards the end of the 4th century, the "second medical revolution"[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-2) took place with the founding of the first Christian hospital in the eastern [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire") by [Basil of Caesarea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basil_of_Caesarea "Basil of Caesarea"), and within a few decades, such hospitals had become ubiquitous in Byzantine society.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-nutton-3) The hospital would undergo development and progress throughout [Byzantine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine "Byzantine"), [medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval "Medieval") European and Islamic societies from the 5th to the 15th century. European exploration brought hospitals to colonies in North America, Africa, and Asia. [St Bartholomew's hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Bartholomew's_Hospital "St Bartholomew's Hospital") in [West Smithfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithfield,_London "Smithfield, London") in London, founded in 1123, is widely considered the oldest functioning hospital today. Originally a charitable institution, currently an NHS hospital it continues to provide free care to Londoners, as it has for 900 years. In contrast, the Mihintale Hospital in [Sri Lanka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sri_Lanka "Sri Lanka"), established in the 9th century is probably the site with the oldest archaeological evidence available for a hospital in the world.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-sri-4) Serving monks and the local community, it represents early advancements in healthcare practices.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-5)

The first Western-style hospital in Japan was established in 1556 by Jesuit missionary [Luis de Almeida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_de_Almeida_(missionary) "Luis de Almeida (missionary)").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-6) Early Chinese and Korean hospitals were founded by Western missionaries in the 1800s.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-8) In the [early modern era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_modern_era "Early modern era") care and healing would transition into a secular affair in the West for many hospitals.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-9) During World War I and World War II, many military hospitals and hospital innovations were created. Government run hospitals increased in Korea, Japan, China, and the Middle East after World War II. In the late 1900s and 21st century, hospital networks and government health organizations were formed to manage groups of hospitals to control costs and share resources. Many smaller, less efficient hospitals in the West were closed because they could not be sustained.

## Antiquity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Antiquity")]

In [ancient history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_history "Ancient history"), [hospitals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hospital "Hospital") have been documented in Greece, Rome, the Indian subcontinent, and Iran. In ancient cultures, religion and medicine were linked.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-10)

### Greece

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Greece")]

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/Patients_sleeping_in_the_temple_of_Aesculapius_at_Epidaurus._Wellcome_V0018154.jpg/250px-Patients_sleeping_in_the_temple_of_Aesculapius_at_Epidaurus._Wellcome_V0018154.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Patients_sleeping_in_the_temple_of_Aesculapius_at_Epidaurus._Wellcome_V0018154.jpg)

Painting depicting patients in an Asclepeion in Ancient Greece

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/Kos_Asklepeion.jpg/250px-Kos_Asklepeion.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kos_Asklepeion.jpg)

View of the _Askleipion_ of [Kos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kos "Kos"), the best preserved instance of a Greek Asklepieion.

In [ancient Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greece "Ancient Greece"), temples dedicated to the healer-god [Asclepius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asclepius "Asclepius"), known as _Asclepieia_ ([Ancient Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀσκληπιεῖα, sing. _Asclepieion_, Ἀσκληπιεῖον), functioned as centres of medical advice, prognosis, and healing.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-Guenter-11) Asclepeia provided carefully controlled spaces conducive to healing and fulfilled several of the requirements of institutions created for healing.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-Guenter-11) Under his Roman name Æsculapius, he was provided with a temple (291 BCE) on an island in the [Tiber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiber "Tiber") in Rome (the [Tiber Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiber_Island "Tiber Island")), where similar rites were performed.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-12)

At these shrines, patients would enter a dream-like state of induced sleep known as _enkoimesis_ (ἐγκοίμησις) not unlike anesthesia, in which they either received guidance from the deity [in a dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleep_temple "Sleep temple").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-Books.Google.com-13) In the Asclepieion of [Epidaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epidaurus "Epidaurus"), three large marble boards dated to 350 BCE preserve the names, case histories, complaints, and cures of about 70 patients who came to the temple with a problem and shed it there. Some of the surgical cures listed, such as the opening of an abdominal abscess or the removal of traumatic foreign material, are realistic enough to have taken place, but with the patient in a state of enkoimesis induced with the help of soporific substances such as opium.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-Books.Google.com-13) The worship of Asclepius was adopted by the [Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome").

The [Athenian Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athenian_military "Athenian military") had a ship named _Therapia_, and the [Roman Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Navy "Roman Navy") had a ship named _Aesculapius_, their names indicating that they may have been hospital ships.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-16)

### Roman Empire

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Roman Empire")]

Further information: [Byzantine medicine §Hospitals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_medicine#Hospitals "Byzantine medicine"), and [Medieval medicine of Western Europe §Hospital system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_medicine_of_Western_Europe#Hospital_system "Medieval medicine of Western Europe")

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/Nlm_nlmuid-101435987-img.jpg/250px-Nlm_nlmuid-101435987-img.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nlm_nlmuid-101435987-img.jpg)

Reconstruction of Roman military hospital at Windisch, Switzerland

The [Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire") constructed buildings called _valetudinaria_ for the care of sick slaves, gladiators, and soldiers around 100 BCE, and many were identified by later archaeology. While their existence is considered proven, there is some doubt as to whether they were as widespread as was once thought, as many were identified only according to the layout of building remains, and not by means of surviving records or finds of medical tools.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-Roman-17)

The declaration of [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") as an accepted religion in the Roman Empire drove an expansion of the provision of care. Following [First Council of Nicaea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Council_of_Nicaea "First Council of Nicaea") in 325 CE construction of a hospital in every [cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathedral "Cathedral") town was begun. Among the earliest were those built by the physician [Saint Sampson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sampson_the_Hospitable "Sampson the Hospitable") in [Constantinople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantinople "Constantinople") and by [Basil of Caesarea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basil_of_Caesarea "Basil of Caesarea") in modern-day Turkey towards the end of the 4th century. By the beginning of the 5th century, the hospital had already become ubiquitous throughout the Christian east in the Byzantine world,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-nutton-3) this being a dramatic shift from the pre-Christian era of the Roman Empire where no civilian hospitals existed.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-clean-1) Called the "[Basilias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basileias "Basileias")", the latter resembled a city and included housing for doctors and nurses and separate buildings for various classes of patients.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-Catholic-18) There was a separate section for lepers.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-19) Some hospitals maintained libraries and training programs, and doctors compiled their medical and pharmacological studies in manuscripts. Thus in-patient medical care in the sense of what we today consider a hospital, was an invention driven by Christian mercy and Byzantine innovation.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-20) Byzantine hospital staff included the [Chief Physician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Physician "Chief Physician") (archiatroi), professional nurses (hypourgoi) and the orderlies (hyperetai). By the twelfth century, Constantinople had two well-organized hospitals, staffed by doctors who were both male and female. Facilities included systematic treatment procedures and specialized wards for various diseases.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-21)

### South & East Asia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: South & East Asia")]

See also: [Ayurveda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayurveda "Ayurveda")

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/Sri_Lankan_Traditional_Medicine.jpg/250px-Sri_Lankan_Traditional_Medicine.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sri_Lankan_Traditional_Medicine.jpg)

[Ruins of a two thousand year old hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Mihintale_Hospital_Complex "Ancient Mihintale Hospital Complex") were discovered in the historical city of [Anuradhapura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anuradhapura "Anuradhapura")[Mihintale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mihintale "Mihintale")[Sri Lanka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sri_Lanka "Sri Lanka")

During the 4th century BCE in ancient [Sri Lanka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sri_Lanka "Sri Lanka"), according to the [Mahāvaṃsa chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mah%C4%81va%E1%B9%83sa "Mahāvaṃsa") from the 6th century CE, King [Pandukabhaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandukabhaya "Pandukabhaya") constructed hospitals and lying-in-homes after fortifying his capital in Anuradhapura. This provides the earliest literary evidence of hospitals, where patients could be housed and treated collectively. The oldest [archaeological evidence of a hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Mihintale_Hospital_Complex "Ancient Mihintale Hospital Complex") in Asia can be found in the ruins of [Mihintale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mihintale "Mihintale"), dating back to the ninth century.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-22) Scholars suggest that this may be one of the oldest hospitals in the world.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-sri-4)

King [Ashoka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashoka_the_Great "Ashoka the Great") is said by many secondary sources to have founded hospitals ca. 230 BCE.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-23) Early medical practices emerged early on in the Indian subcontinent with the practice of [Ayurvedic medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayurveda "Ayurveda"), one of the earliest texts for which survive being the [Charaka Samhita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charaka_Samhita "Charaka Samhita") and [Sushruta Samhita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sushruta_Samhita "Sushruta Samhita"). Some early [Buddhist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism "Buddhism") communities established monastic communities with monasteries, and many of these monasteries were centers of learning for medicine. While sick monks within the monastic communities were usually treated in their own cells, some monasteries reserved a room where sick monks could be taken care of.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-24) While some of these rooms in Buddhist monasteries may have been open to the public, the majority were closed off to the public and were reserved for treating other monks within the monastery.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-26) This ideal is reflected in the story of the monk with dysentery.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-27) The first clear reference to an actual hospital within the southeast Asian world occurs in the accounts of the traveller [Fa Xian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fa_Xian "Fa Xian") in the 5th century CE, who describes hospitals in the city of [Pataliputra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pataliputra "Pataliputra") and a few other sites:

> The benevolent and educated persons of this country have instituted a free hospital within the city; and hither come all poor or helpless inhabitants suffering from all kinds of infirmities. They are well taken care of, and a doctor attends them, food and medicine being supplied according to their wants. Thus they are made quite comfortable, and when they are well they may go away.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-28)

The first clear archaeological evidence of such hospitals first appears in the eighth and ninth centuries. Nevertheless, it would be inaccurate to portray the period as a time when a system of hospitals had existed. Rather, rulers from time to time may have sponsored and allocated resources for particular medical care for the population in particular places.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-29) In one case, a countrywide system of hospitals was established in 12th century [Cambodia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambodia "Cambodia") under the Cambodian king [Jayavarman VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jayavarman_VII "Jayavarman VII"), who associated it with the Buddha of healing [Bhaisajyaguru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhaisajyaguru "Bhaisajyaguru").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-30)

Significant and asymmetric transfers of knowledge to the southeast Asian world from the Greek one began during the reign of [Alexander the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_the_Great "Alexander the Great") in the late 4th century BCE as [Hellenization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellenization "Hellenization") swept the continent.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-31) While usually assumed that [Tibetan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibet "Tibet") medicine was largely Chinese in origin, it turns out that Tibetan medicine was actually largely Westernized, at least during the first century of the [Tibetan Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibetan_Empire "Tibetan Empire") in the 7th–8th centuries. Persian and Arab doctors from the Islamic Caliphate could be found all across [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") in this time period.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-32) It's also possible that Indian physicians played a role in a short-lived, but still one of the earliest Abbasid hospitals established by the Barkamid family.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-33)

In the [Medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages") period the term _hospital_ encompassed hostels for travellers, dispensaries for [poor relief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poor_relief "Poor relief"), clinics and surgeries for the injured, and homes for the blind, lame, elderly, and mentally ill. [Monastic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monastic "Monastic") hospitals developed many treatments, both therapeutic and spiritual.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-Miller-35)

During the thirteenth century an immense number of hospitals were built. The [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy") cities were the leaders of the movement. [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan "Milan") had no fewer than a dozen hospitals and [Florence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence "Florence") before the end of the fourteenth century had some thirty hospitals. Some of these were very beautiful buildings. At Milan a portion of the general hospital was designed by [Bramante](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donato_Bramante "Donato Bramante") and another part of it by [Michelangelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelangelo "Michelangelo"). The Hospital of [Siena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siena "Siena"), built in honor of [St. Catherine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_of_Siena "Catherine of Siena"), has been famous ever since. Everywhere throughout Europe this hospital movement spread. [Virchow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Virchow "Rudolf Virchow"), the great German pathologist, in an article on hospitals, showed that every city of Germany of five thousand inhabitants had its hospital. He traced all of this hospital movement to [Pope Innocent III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Innocent_III "Pope Innocent III"), and though he was least papistically inclined, Virchow did not hesitate to give extremely high praise to this pontiff for all that he had accomplished for the benefit of children and suffering mankind.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-63)

Hospitals began to appear in great numbers in [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") and [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England"). Following the [French Norman invasion into England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_conquest_of_England "Norman conquest of England"), the explosion of French ideals led most Medieval monasteries to develop a hospitium or hospice for pilgrims. This hospitium eventually developed into what we now understand as a hospital, with various monks and lay helpers providing the medical care for sick pilgrims and victims of the numerous plagues and chronic diseases that afflicted Medieval Western Europe. Benjamin Gordon supports the theory that the hospital – as we know it – is a French invention, but that it was originally developed for isolating [lepers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leper "Leper") and plague victims, and only later undergoing modification to serve the pilgrim.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-64)

Owing to a well-preserved 12th-century account of the monk [Eadmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eadmer "Eadmer") of the Canterbury cathedral, there is an excellent account of [Bishop Lanfranc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_Lanfranc?action=edit&redlink=1 "Bishop Lanfranc (page does not exist)")'s aim to establish and maintain examples of these early hospitals:

> But I must not conclude my work by omitting what he did for the poor outside the walls of the city Canterbury. In brief, he constructed a decent and ample house of stone...for different needs and conveniences. He divided the main building into two, appointing one part for men oppressed by various kinds of infirmities and the other for women in a bad state of health. He also made arrangements for their clothing and daily food, appointing ministers and guardians to take all measures so that nothing should be lacking for them.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-65)

### India

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: India")]

During the [Chola Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chola_Empire "Chola Empire") (9th to 13th centuries CE), health care was institutionalized via state-supported village dispensaries and hospitals alternatively referred to in [epigraphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epigraphy "Epigraphy") as _atulasalai_ or _vaidyasalai_.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-IndianScience-66) These facilities were commonly integrated into local temple economies and sustained via _vaittiyavritti_—royal land grants specifically allocated to hereditary medical practitioners.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-IndianScience-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-Reddy-67)

The most complete operational blueprint of a Chola medical center comes from a 1067 CE inscription commissioned by Emperor [Veera Rajendra Chola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virarajendra "Virarajendra") at the Venkateswara temple in Tirumukkudal.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-Somasundaram2014-68) The inscription details the Veera Cholesvara Hospital, a 15-bed institutional infirmary that provided Ayurvedic and [Siddha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siddha_medicine "Siddha medicine") care to students, teachers, and temple members.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-Somasundaram2014-68) The staff followed a strict institutional hierarchy, consisting of a chief physician, a [surgeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surgeon "Surgeon"), two male [herbalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbalist "Herbalist"), two female nurses responsible for feeding and dosage preparation, a barber, a washerman, and a waterman.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-IndianScience-66)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-Desousa2018-69)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-Reddy-67)

### Persia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Persia")]

The [Academy of Gondishapur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Gondishapur "Academy of Gondishapur") was a hospital and medical training center at [Gundeshapur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gundeshapur "Gundeshapur") in [Persia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persia "Persia"). The city of Gundeshapur was founded in 271 CE by the [Sasanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sasanian_Empire "Sasanian Empire") king [Shapur I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shapur_I "Shapur I"). It was one of the major cities in [Khuzestan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khuzestan_province "Khuzestan province") province of the Persian empire, in Iran. A large percentage of the population were [Syriacs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syriac_Christians "Syriac Christians"), most of whom were Christians. Under the rule of [Khosrow I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khosrow_I "Khosrow I"), refuge was granted to Greek [Nestorian Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nestorianism "Nestorianism") philosophers including the scholars of the Persian School of [Edessa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edessa "Edessa") ([Urfa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urfa "Urfa")) (also called the Academy of Athens), a Christian theological and medical university. These scholars made their way to Gundeshapur in 529 following the closing of the academy by Emperor [Justinian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justinian_I "Justinian I"). They were engaged in medical sciences and initiated the first translation projects of medical texts.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-70) The arrival of these medical practitioners from Edessa marks the beginning of the hospital and medical centre at Gundeshapur.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-Taylor-34) It included a medical school and hospital ([bimaristan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bimaristan "Bimaristan")), a pharmacology laboratory, a translation house, a library and an observatory.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-71) Indian doctors also contributed to the school at Gundeshapur, most notably the medical researcher Mankah. Following the [Muslim conquest of Persia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_conquest_of_Persia "Muslim conquest of Persia") in the 7th century, the writings of [Mankah (Ancient Indian physician)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mankah_(Ancient_Indian_physician) "Mankah (Ancient Indian physician)") and of the ancient Indian physician and surgeon [Sushruta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sushruta "Sushruta") were translated into Arabic at [Baghdad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baghdad "Baghdad")'s [House of Wisdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Wisdom "House of Wisdom").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-72)

### Medieval Islamic hospitals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Medieval Islamic hospitals")]

Main articles: [Medicine in the medieval Islamic world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicine_in_the_medieval_Islamic_world "Medicine in the medieval Islamic world") and [Bimaristan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bimaristan "Bimaristan")

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Door_of_the_Moristan_of_Kala%27oon_%281878%29_-_TIMEA.jpg/250px-Door_of_the_Moristan_of_Kala%27oon_%281878%29_-_TIMEA.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Door_of_the_Moristan_of_Kala'oon_(1878)_-_TIMEA.jpg)

Entrance to the [Qalawun complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qalawun_complex "Qalawun complex") in Cairo, Egypt which housed the notable Mansuri hospital.

The first Muslim hospital was an asylum to contain leprosy, built in the early eighth century, where patients were confined but, like the blind, were given a stipend to support their families.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-aramco0317-73) The earliest general hospital was built in 805 CE in Baghdad by Harun Al-Rashid.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-Glubb-75) By the tenth century, Baghdad had five more hospitals, while [Damascus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damascus "Damascus") had six hospitals by the 15th century and [Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%B3rdoba,_Andalusia "Córdoba, Andalusia") alone had 50 major hospitals, many exclusively for the military.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-aramco0317-73) Many of the prominent early [Islamic hospitals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bimaristan "Bimaristan") were founded with assistance by Christians such as [Jibrael ibn Bukhtishu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jabril_ibn_Bukhtishu "Jabril ibn Bukhtishu") from [Gundeshapur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gundeshapur "Gundeshapur").[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-77) "[Bimaristan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bimaristan "Bimaristan")" is a compound of "bimar" (sick or ill) and "stan" (place). In the [medieval Islamic world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_Golden_Age "Islamic Golden Age"), the word "bimaristan" referred to a hospital establishment where the ill were welcomed, cared for and treated by qualified staff.

The [United States National Library of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Library_of_Medicine "United States National Library of Medicine") credits the hospital as being a product of [medieval Islamic civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_Golden_Age "Islamic Golden Age"). Compared to contemporaneous Christian institutions, which were poor and sick relief facilities offered by some monasteries, the Islamic hospital was a more elaborate institution with a wider range of functions. In [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam"), there was a moral imperative to treat the ill regardless of financial status. Islamic hospitals tended to be large, urban structures, and were largely secular institutions, many open to all, whether male or female, civilian or military, child or adult, rich or poor, Muslim or non-Muslim. The Islamic hospital served several purposes, as a center of medical treatment, a home for patients recovering from illness or accidents, an insane asylum, and a retirement home with basic maintenance needs for the aged and infirm.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-nlm-78)

The typical hospital was divided into departments such as systemic diseases, surgery and orthopedics with larger hospitals having more diverse specialties. "Systemic diseases" was the rough equivalent of today's [internal medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_medicine "Internal medicine") and was further divided into sections such as fever, infections and digestive issues. Every department had an officer-in-charge, a presiding officer and a supervising specialist. The hospitals also had lecture theaters and libraries. Hospitals staff included sanitary inspectors, who regulated cleanliness, and accountants and other administrative staff.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-aramco0317-73) The hospital in Baghdad employed twenty-five staff physicians.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-79) The hospitals were typically run by a three-man board comprising a non-medical administrator, the chief pharmacist, called the shaykh saydalani, who was equal in rank to the chief physician, who served as mutwalli (dean).[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-aramco-80) Medical facilities traditionally closed each night, but by the 10th century laws were passed to keep hospitals open 24 hours a day.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-sdouglas-81)

For less serious cases, physicians staffed outpatient clinics. Cities also had first aid centers staffed by physicians for emergencies that were often located in busy public places, such as big gatherings for Friday prayers to take care of casualties. The region also had mobile units staffed by doctors and pharmacists who were supposed to meet the need of remote communities. Baghdad was also known to have a separate hospital for convicts since the early 10th century after the vizier 'Ali ibn Isa ibn Jarah ibn Thabit wrote to Baghdad's chief medical officer that "prisons must have their own doctors who should examine them every day". The first hospital built in Egypt, in Cairo's Southwestern quarter, was the first documented facility to care for [mental illnesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychology_in_medieval_Islam "Psychology in medieval Islam") while the first Islamic [psychiatric hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychiatric_hospital "Psychiatric hospital") opened in Baghdad in 705.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-Medicine_And_Health-82)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-aramco0317-73)

Medical students would accompany physicians and participate in patient care. Hospitals in this era were the first to require medical diplomas to license doctors.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-Alatas-83) The licensing test was administered by the region's government appointed chief medical officer. The test had two steps; the first was to write a treatise, on the subject the candidate wished to obtain a certificate, of original research or commentary of existing texts, which they were encouraged to scrutinize for errors. The second step was to answer questions in an interview with the chief medical officer. Physicians worked fixed hours and medical staff salaries were fixed by law. For regulating the quality of care and arbitrating cases, it is related that if a patient dies, their family presents the doctor's prescriptions to the chief physician who would judge if the death was natural or if it was by negligence, in which case the family would be entitled to compensation from the doctor. The hospitals had male and female quarters while some hospitals only saw men and other hospitals, staffed by women physicians, only saw women.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-aramco0317-73) While women physicians practiced medicine, many largely focused on [obstetrics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obstetrics "Obstetrics").[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-aramco0816-84)

Hospitals were forbidden by law to turn away patients who were unable to pay.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-sdouglas-81) Eventually, [charitable foundations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charitable_foundation "Charitable foundation") called [waqfs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waqf "Waqf") were formed to support hospitals, as well as schools.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-sdouglas-81) Part of the state budget also went towards maintaining hospitals.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-aramco0317-73) While the services of the hospital were free for all citizens[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-sdouglas-81) and patients were sometimes given a small stipend to support recovery upon discharge, individual physicians occasionally charged fees.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-aramco0317-73) In a notable endowment, a 13th-century governor of Egypt [Al Mansur Qalawun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Mansur_Qalawun "Al Mansur Qalawun") ordained a foundation for the [Qalawun hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qalawun_complex "Qalawun complex") that would contain a mosque and a chapel, separate wards for different diseases, a library for doctors and a pharmacy[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-adler-85) and the hospital is used today for [ophthalmology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ophthalmology "Ophthalmology").[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-aramco0317-73) The Qalawun hospital was based in a former Fatimid palace which had accommodation for 8,000 people -[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-86) "it served 4,000 patients daily."[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-87) The waqf stated,

> _...The hospital shall keep all patients, men and women, until they are completely recovered. All costs are to be borne by the hospital whether the people come from afar or near, whether they are residents or foreigners, strong or weak, low or high, rich or poor, employed or unemployed, blind or sighted, physically or mentally ill, learned or illiterate. There are no conditions of consideration and payment, none is objected to or even indirectly hinted at for non-payment._[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-adler-85)

The first, most well known physicians in the Medieval Islamic world were polymaths Ibn Sina, (Greek: Avicenna) and Al Rhazi (Greek: Rhazes) during the 10th and 11th centuries.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-88)

### Medieval European hospitals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Medieval European hospitals")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/LesInvalidesFull.JPG/250px-LesInvalidesFull.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:LesInvalidesFull.JPG)

The church at [Les Invalides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Invalides "Les Invalides") in Paris, showing the typically close connection between hospitals and the Catholic church

Medieval hospitals in Europe followed a similar pattern to the [Byzantine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine "Byzantine"). They were religious communities, with care provided by [monks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monk "Monk") and [nuns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nun "Nun"). An old French term for hospital is _hôtel-Dieu_, "hostel of God."[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-89) Some were attached to monasteries; others were independent and had their own endowments, usually of property, which provided income for their support. Some hospitals were multi-functional while others were founded for specific purposes such as leper hospitals, or as refuges for the poor, or for [pilgrims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilgrim "Pilgrim"): not all cared for the sick.

Around 529 CE St. [Benedict of Nursia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benedict_of_Nursia "Benedict of Nursia") (480–543 CE), later a Christian saint, the founder of western [monasticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monasticism "Monasticism") and the [Order of St. Benedict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_St._Benedict "Order of St. Benedict"), today the [patron saint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patron_saint "Patron saint") of Europe, established the first [monastery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monastery "Monastery") in Europe ([Monte Cassino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Cassino "Monte Cassino")) on a hilltop between [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome") and [Naples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naples "Naples"), that became a model for the Western monasticism and one of the major cultural centers of Europe throughout the Middle Ages. St. Benedict wrote the [Rule of Saint Benedict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_of_Saint_Benedict "Rule of Saint Benedict") which mandated the moral obligations to care for the sick.

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Charles_Marville%2C_L%E2%80%99H%C3%B4tel-Dieu%2C_du_quai_Saint_Michel._Paris_IVe._Vers_1867_-_Vergue.jpg/250px-Charles_Marville%2C_L%E2%80%99H%C3%B4tel-Dieu%2C_du_quai_Saint_Michel._Paris_IVe._Vers_1867_-_Vergue.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Charles_Marville,_L%E2%80%99H%C3%B4tel-Dieu,_du_quai_Saint_Michel._Paris_IVe._Vers_1867_-_Vergue.jpg)

[Hôtel-Dieu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%B4tel-Dieu_de_Paris "Hôtel-Dieu de Paris") of Paris.

The first Spanish hospital, founded by the Catholic [Visigoth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visigoth "Visigoth") bishop [Masona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masona "Masona") in 580 CE at [Mérida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%A9rida,_Spain "Mérida, Spain"), was a _[xenodochium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xenodochium "Xenodochium")_ designed as an inn for travellers (mostly pilgrims to the shrine of [Eulalia of Mérida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eulalia_of_M%C3%A9rida "Eulalia of Mérida")) as well as a hospital for citizens and local farmers. The hospital's endowment consisted of farms to feed its patients and guests. From the account given by [Paul the Deacon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_the_Deacon "Paul the Deacon") we learn that this hospital was supplied with physicians and nurses, whose mission included the care the sick wherever they were found, "slave or free, Christian or Jew."[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-90) In 650, the "[Hôtel-Dieu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%B4tel-Dieu_de_Paris "Hôtel-Dieu de Paris")" was found in Paris,[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-London_Science_Museum-91) but its first recorded mention only dates back to 829,[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-New_Catholic_Encyclopedia_p._127-92) it is considered by many as the oldest worldwide hospital still operating today.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-Pioneers-93) It was a multipurpose institution which catered for the sick and poor, offering shelter, food and medical care.

During the late 8th and early 9th centuries, Emperor Charlemagne decreed that those hospitals that had been well conducted before his time and had fallen into decay should be restored in accordance with the needs of the time.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-capitulary_duplex_803_iii-94) He further ordered that a hospital should be attached to each cathedral and monastery.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-capitulary_duplex_803_iii-94)

During the 10th century, the monasteries became a dominant factor in hospital work. The famous Benedictine Abbey of Cluny, founded in 910, set the example which was widely imitated throughout France and Germany.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-95) Besides its infirmary for the religious, each monastery had a hospital in which externs were cared for. These were in charge of the _eleemosynarius_, whose duties, carefully prescribed by the rule, included every sort of service that the visitor or patient could require.

As the eleemosynarius was obliged to seek out the sick and needy in the neighborhood, each monastery became a center for the relief of suffering. Among the monasteries notable in this respect were those of the Benedictines at Corbie in Picardy, Hirschau, Braunweiler, Deutz, Ilsenburg, Liesborn, Pram, and Fulda; those of the Cistercians at Arnsberg, Baumgarten, Eberbach, Himmenrode, Herrnalb, Volkenrode, and Walkenried.

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/Hotel_Dieu_in_Paris_about_1500.gif/500px-Hotel_Dieu_in_Paris_about_1500.gif?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hotel_Dieu_in_Paris_about_1500.gif)

[Hôtel-Dieu de Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%B4tel-Dieu_de_Paris "Hôtel-Dieu de Paris") c. 1500. The comparatively well patients (on the right) were separated from the very ill (on the left).

No less efficient was the work done by the [diocesan clergy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocese "Diocese") in accordance with the disciplinary enactments of the councils of Aachen (817, 836), which prescribed that a hospital should be maintained in connection with each collegiate church. The canons were obliged to contribute towards the support of the hospital, and one of their number had charge of the inmates. As these hospitals were located in cities, more numerous demands were made upon them than upon those attached to the monasteries. In this movement the [bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop "Bishop") naturally took the lead, hence the hospitals founded by [Heribert of Cologne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heribert_of_Cologne "Heribert of Cologne") (d. 1021) in [Cologne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cologne "Cologne"), [Godard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gotthard_of_Hildesheim "Gotthard of Hildesheim") (d. 1038) in [Hildesheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hildesheim "Hildesheim"), [Conrad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conrad_of_Constance "Conrad of Constance") (d. 975) in [Constance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konstanz "Konstanz"), and [Ulrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulrich "Ulrich") (d. 973) in [Augsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augsburg "Augsburg"). But similar provision was made by the other churches; thus at [Trier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trier "Trier") the hospitals of [Saint Maximin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximin_of_Trier "Maximin of Trier"), [Saint Matthew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Matthew "Saint Matthew"), [Saint Simeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Peter "Simon Peter"), and [Saint James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_the_Just "James the Just") took their names from the churches to which they were attached. During the period 1207–1577 no less than one hundred and fifty-five hospitals were founded in Germany.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-96)

The [Ospedale Maggiore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ospedale_Maggiore "Ospedale Maggiore"), traditionally named Ca' Granda (i.e. Big House), in [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan "Milan"), northern Italy, was constructed to house one of the first community hospitals, the largest such undertaking of the fifteenth century. Commissioned by [Francesco Sforza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Sforza "Francesco Sforza") in 1456 and designed by [Antonio Filarete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Filarete "Antonio Filarete") it is among the first examples of Renaissance architecture in Lombardy.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-Italy-38)

The Normans brought their hospital system along when they conquered England in 1066. By merging with traditional land-tenure and customs, the new charitable houses became popular and were distinct from both English monasteries and French hospitals. They dispensed alms and some medicine, and were generously endowed by the nobility and gentry who counted on them for spiritual rewards after death.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-97)

### Late medieval European hospitals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Late medieval European hospitals")]

The Hospitaller Order of St. John of Jerusalem, founded in 1099 (The Knights of Malta) itself has – as its raison d'être – the founding of a hospital for pilgrims to the Holy Land. In Europe, Spanish hospitals are particularly noteworthy examples of Christian virtue as expressed through care for the sick, and were usually attached to a monastery in a ward-chapel configuration, most often erected in the shape of a cross. This style reached a high point during the hospital building campaign of Portuguese St. John of God in the sixteenth-century, the founder of the Hospitaller Order of the Brothers of John of God.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-98)

Soon many monasteries were founded throughout Europe, and everywhere there were hospitals like in Monte Cassino. By the 11th century, some monasteries were training their own physicians. Ideally, such physicians would uphold the Christianized ideal of the healer who offered mercy and charity towards all patients and soldiers, whatever their status and prognosis might be. In the 6th–12th centuries the Benedictines established many monk communities of this type. And later, in the 12th–13th centuries the Benedictines order built a network of independent hospitals, initially to provide general care to the sick and wounded and then for treatment of syphilis and isolation of patients with communicable disease. The hospital movement spread through Europe in the subsequent centuries, with a 225-bed hospital being built at York in 1287 and even larger facilities established at Florence, Paris, Milan, Siena, and other medieval big European cities. In 1120 a man named Rahere fell ill with malaria in Rome: he was taken care of by the monks of the small hospital near the church of San Bartolomeo, on the Tiber Island, and took a vow to found a hospital in case he was cured. Effectively cured, in 1123 he founded a small hospital for the poor outside London: it was the first nucleus of the famous [St Bartholomew's Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Bartholomew's_Hospital "St Bartholomew's Hospital"), still active today, commonly called "Bart".

In the North during the late Saxon period, monasteries, nunneries, and hospitals functioned mainly as a site of charity to the poor. After the [Norman Conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_conquest_of_England "Norman conquest of England") of 1066, hospitals are found to be autonomous, freestanding institutions. They dispensed alms and some medicine, and were generously endowed by the nobility and gentry who counted on them for spiritual rewards after death.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-99) In time, hospitals became popular charitable houses that were distinct from both English monasteries and French hospitals.

The primary function of medieval hospitals was to worship to God. Most hospitals contained one chapel, at least one clergyman, and inmates that were expected to help with prayer. Worship was often a higher priority than care and was a large part of hospital life until and long after the [Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Reformation "English Reformation"). Worship in medieval hospitals served as a way of alleviating ailments of the sick and insuring their salvation when relief from sickness could not be achieved.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-English_Hospital-100)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-Bowers-101)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/34/The_ruins_of_St._Giles_Leper_Hospital_-_geograph.org.uk_-_834044.jpg/250px-The_ruins_of_St._Giles_Leper_Hospital_-_geograph.org.uk_-_834044.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_ruins_of_St._Giles_Leper_Hospital_-_geograph.org.uk_-_834044.jpg)

Ruins of [St. Giles Hospital (Great Hospital)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Hospital "Great Hospital")

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/Remains_of_St_Leonards_Hospital%2C_York_-_panoramio.jpg/250px-Remains_of_St_Leonards_Hospital%2C_York_-_panoramio.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Remains_of_St_Leonards_Hospital,_York_-_panoramio.jpg)

Ruins of St Leonard's Hospital.

The secondary function of medieval hospitals was charity to the poor, sick, and travellers.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-102) Charity provided by hospitals surfaced in different ways, including long-term maintenance of the infirm, medium-term care of the sick, short-term hospitality to travellers, and regular distribution of alms to the poor.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-English_Hospital-100):58 Though these were general acts of charity among medieval hospitals, the degree of charity was variable. For example, some institutions that perceived themselves mainly as a religious house or place of hospitality turned away the sick or dying in fear that difficult healthcare will distract from worship. Others, however, such as St. James of Northallerton, [St. Giles Hospital of Norwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Hospital "Great Hospital"), and [St. Leonard's Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York_Museum_Gardens#Medieval "York Museum Gardens") of York, contained specific ordinances stating they must cater to the sick and that "all who entered with ill health should be allowed to stay until they recovered or died".[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-English_Hospital-100):58[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-Hospital_Life-103):23 The study of these three hospitals provides insight into the diet, medical care, cleanliness and daily life in a medieval hospital of Europe.

The tertiary function of medieval hospitals was to support education and learning. Originally, hospitals educated chaplains and priestly brothers in literacy and history; however, by the 13th century, some hospitals became involved in the education of impoverished boys and young adults. Soon after, hospitals began to provide food and shelter for scholars within the hospital in return for helping with chapel worship.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-English_Hospital-100):65

## 16th and 17th centuries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: 16th and 17th centuries")]

**Notable hospitals in the 16th and 17th centuries with articles in Wikipedia**

[16th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Hospitals_established_in_the_16th_century "Category:Hospitals established in the 16th century") (19)[17th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Hospitals_established_in_the_17th_century "Category:Hospitals established in the 17th century") (22)

### Early modern Europe

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Early modern Europe")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/Physician_in_hospital_sickroom_printed_1682.jpg/250px-Physician_in_hospital_sickroom_printed_1682.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Physician_in_hospital_sickroom_printed_1682.jpg)

A physician visiting the [sick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disease "Disease") in a hospital, German [engraving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engraving "Engraving") from 1682

In Europe the medieval concept of Christian care evolved during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries into a secular one.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-104) Theology was the problem. The Protestant reformers rejected the Catholic belief that rich men could gain God's grace through good works – and escape purgatory – by providing endowments to charitable institutions, and that the patients themselves could gain grace through their suffering.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-105)

After the [dissolution of the monasteries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_monasteries "Dissolution of the monasteries") in 1540 by King [Henry VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VIII "Henry VIII") the church abruptly ceased to be the supporter of hospitals, and only by direct petition from the citizens of [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), were the hospitals [St Bartholomew's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Bartholomew's_Hospital "St Bartholomew's Hospital"), [St Thomas's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Thomas's_Hospital "St Thomas's Hospital") and [St Mary of Bethlehem's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethlem_Royal_Hospital "Bethlem Royal Hospital") (Bedlam) endowed directly by the crown.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-106) It was at St. Bartholomew that [William Harvey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Harvey "William Harvey") conducted his research on the circulatory system in the 17th century, [Percivall Pott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percivall_Pott "Percivall Pott") and [John Abernethy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Abernethy_(surgeon) "John Abernethy (surgeon)") developed important principles of modern surgery in the 18th century, and Mrs. Bedford Fenwich worked to advance the nursing profession in the late 19th century.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-107)

There were 28 asylums in [Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden "Sweden") at the start of the [Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformation "Reformation"). [Gustav Vasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_Vasa "Gustav Vasa") removed them from church control and expelled the monks and nuns, but allowed the asylums to keep their properties and to continue their activities under the auspices of local government.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-108)

In much of Europe town governments operated small Holy Spirit hospitals, which had been founded in the 13th and 14th centuries. They distributed free food and clothing to the poor, provided for homeless women and children, and gave some medical and nursing care. Many were raided and closed during the [Thirty Years War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty_Years_War "Thirty Years War") (1618–48), which ravaged the towns and villages of Germany and neighboring areas for three decades.

In Denmark, the beginnings of modern hospital care started during the [Scanian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scanian_War "Scanian War") (1675–79) when Denmark suffered disastrous losses. Five government-run hospitals were founded around the Sound: one at Elsinore, two at Copenhagen, one at Landskrona and one at Helsingborg. The one at Landskrona was based on the old Holy Spirit institution but now it was modernised and enlarged. One of the two Copenhagen institutions was placed in a former plague hospital. The government spent vast sums on equipment, from bone saws to beds and staff. Women nursed the wounded and sick soldiers on a day-to-day basis but men were always head of these hospitals. They had various surgeons and physicians, but never enough of them. The meals were based on porridge, herring, beer and peas. After Denmark lost the war, Helsingborg and Landskrona were surrendered to the Swedes but the hospitals in Elsinore and Copenhagen continued their work.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-109)

Meanwhile, in Catholic lands such as [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") and [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"), rich families continued to fund convents and monasteries that provided free health services to the poor. French practices were influenced by a charitable imperative which considered care of the poor and the sick to be a necessary part of Catholic practice.
