[16th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Hospitals_established_in_the_16th_century "Category:Hospitals established in the 16th century") (19)[17th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Hospitals_established_in_the_17th_century "Category:Hospitals established in the 17th century") (22)

### Early modern Europe

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Early modern Europe")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/Physician_in_hospital_sickroom_printed_1682.jpg/250px-Physician_in_hospital_sickroom_printed_1682.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Physician_in_hospital_sickroom_printed_1682.jpg)

A physician visiting the [sick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disease "Disease") in a hospital, German [engraving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engraving "Engraving") from 1682

In Europe the medieval concept of Christian care evolved during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries into a secular one.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-104) Theology was the problem. The Protestant reformers rejected the Catholic belief that rich men could gain God's grace through good works – and escape purgatory – by providing endowments to charitable institutions, and that the patients themselves could gain grace through their suffering.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-105)

After the [dissolution of the monasteries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_monasteries "Dissolution of the monasteries") in 1540 by King [Henry VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VIII "Henry VIII") the church abruptly ceased to be the supporter of hospitals, and only by direct petition from the citizens of [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), were the hospitals [St Bartholomew's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Bartholomew's_Hospital "St Bartholomew's Hospital"), [St Thomas's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Thomas's_Hospital "St Thomas's Hospital") and [St Mary of Bethlehem's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethlem_Royal_Hospital "Bethlem Royal Hospital") (Bedlam) endowed directly by the crown.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-106) It was at St. Bartholomew that [William Harvey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Harvey "William Harvey") conducted his research on the circulatory system in the 17th century, [Percivall Pott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percivall_Pott "Percivall Pott") and [John Abernethy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Abernethy_(surgeon) "John Abernethy (surgeon)") developed important principles of modern surgery in the 18th century, and Mrs. Bedford Fenwich worked to advance the nursing profession in the late 19th century.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-107)

There were 28 asylums in [Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden "Sweden") at the start of the [Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformation "Reformation"). [Gustav Vasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_Vasa "Gustav Vasa") removed them from church control and expelled the monks and nuns, but allowed the asylums to keep their properties and to continue their activities under the auspices of local government.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-108)

In much of Europe town governments operated small Holy Spirit hospitals, which had been founded in the 13th and 14th centuries. They distributed free food and clothing to the poor, provided for homeless women and children, and gave some medical and nursing care. Many were raided and closed during the [Thirty Years War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty_Years_War "Thirty Years War") (1618–48), which ravaged the towns and villages of Germany and neighboring areas for three decades.

In Denmark, the beginnings of modern hospital care started during the [Scanian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scanian_War "Scanian War") (1675–79) when Denmark suffered disastrous losses. Five government-run hospitals were founded around the Sound: one at Elsinore, two at Copenhagen, one at Landskrona and one at Helsingborg. The one at Landskrona was based on the old Holy Spirit institution but now it was modernised and enlarged. One of the two Copenhagen institutions was placed in a former plague hospital. The government spent vast sums on equipment, from bone saws to beds and staff. Women nursed the wounded and sick soldiers on a day-to-day basis but men were always head of these hospitals. They had various surgeons and physicians, but never enough of them. The meals were based on porridge, herring, beer and peas. After Denmark lost the war, Helsingborg and Landskrona were surrendered to the Swedes but the hospitals in Elsinore and Copenhagen continued their work.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-109)

Meanwhile, in Catholic lands such as [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") and [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"), rich families continued to fund convents and monasteries that provided free health services to the poor. French practices were influenced by a charitable imperative which considered care of the poor and the sick to be a necessary part of Catholic practice. The nursing nuns had little faith in the power of physicians and their medicines alone to cure the sick; more important was providing psychological and physical comfort, nourishment, rest, cleanliness and especially prayer.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-110)

In Protestant areas the emphasis was on scientific rather than religious aspects of patient care, and this helped develop a view of nursing as a profession rather than a vocation.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-111) There was little hospital development by the main Protestant churches after 1530.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-112) Some smaller groups such as the Moravians and the Pietists at Halle gave a role for hospitals, especially in missionary work.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-113)

### Colonial Americas

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Colonial Americas")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Hospicio_Caba%C3%B1as.JPG/250px-Hospicio_Caba%C3%B1as.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hospicio_Caba%C3%B1as.JPG)

[Hospicio Cabañas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hospicio_Caba%C3%B1as "Hospicio Cabañas") was the largest hospital in colonial America, in [Guadalajara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guadalajara "Guadalajara"), Mexico

The first hospital founded in the Americas was the [Hospital San Nicolás de Bari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hospital_San_Nicol%C3%A1s_de_Bari "Hospital San Nicolás de Bari") in [Santo Domingo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santo_Domingo "Santo Domingo"), [Distrito Nacional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distrito_Nacional "Distrito Nacional")[Dominican Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominican_Republic "Dominican Republic"). Fray [Nicolás de Ovando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicol%C3%A1s_de_Ovando "Nicolás de Ovando"), Spanish governor and colonial administrator from 1502 to 1509, authorized its construction on December 29, 1503. This hospital apparently incorporated a church. The first phase of its construction was completed in 1519, and it was rebuilt in 1552.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-Micheli_2005_p._59-114) Abandoned in the mid-18th century, the hospital now lies in ruins near the [Basilica Cathedral of Santa María la Menor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilica_Cathedral_of_Santa_Mar%C3%ADa_la_Menor "Basilica Cathedral of Santa María la Menor") in Santo Domingo.

[Conquistador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquistador "Conquistador")[Hernán Cortés](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hern%C3%A1n_Cort%C3%A9s "Hernán Cortés") founded the two earliest hospitals in North America: the Immaculate Conception Hospital and the Saint Lazarus Hospital. The oldest was the Immaculate Conception, now the [Hospital de Jesús Nazareno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hospital_de_Jes%C3%BAs_Nazareno "Hospital de Jesús Nazareno") in [Mexico City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City "Mexico City"), founded in 1524 to care for the poor.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-Micheli_2005_p._59-114)

In Quebec, Catholics operated hospitals continuously from the 1640s; they attracted nuns from the provincial elite. [Jeanne Mance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_Mance "Jeanne Mance") (1606–73) founded Montreal's city's first hospital, the [Hôtel-Dieu de Montréal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%B4tel-Dieu_de_Montr%C3%A9al "Hôtel-Dieu de Montréal"), in 1645. In 1657 she recruited three sisters of the [Religious Hospitallers of St. Joseph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_Hospitallers_of_St._Joseph "Religious Hospitallers of St. Joseph"), and continued to direct operations of the hospital. The project, begun by the niece of [Cardinal de Richelieu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_de_Richelieu "Cardinal de Richelieu") was granted a royal charter by King [Louis XIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XIII "Louis XIII") and staffed by a colonial physician, [Robert Giffard de Moncel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Giffard_de_Moncel "Robert Giffard de Moncel").[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-115) The General Hospital in Quebec City opened in 1692. They often handled malaria, dysentery, and respiratory sickness.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-116)

## 18th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: 18th century")]

See also: [Category:Hospitals established in the 18th century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Hospitals_established_in_the_18th_century "Category:Hospitals established in the 18th century")

In the 18th century, under the influence of the [Age of Enlightenment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment "Age of Enlightenment"), the modern hospital began to appear, serving only medical needs and staffed with trained physicians and surgeons. The nurses were untrained workers. The goal was to use modern methods to cure patients. They provided more narrow medical services, and were founded by the secular authorities. A clearer distinction emerged between medicine and poor relief. Within the hospitals, acute cases were increasingly treated alone, and separate departments were set up for different categories of patient.

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/Guy%27s_Hospital00.jpg/250px-Guy%27s_Hospital00.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Guy's_Hospital00.jpg)

1820 Engraving of [Guy's Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guy's_Hospital "Guy's Hospital") in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") one of the first voluntary hospitals to be established in 1724.

The voluntary hospital movement began in the early 18th century, with hospitals being founded in London by the 1710s and 20s, including [Westminster Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_Hospital "Westminster Hospital") (1719) promoted by the [private bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_bank "Private bank")[C. Hoare & Co](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._Hoare_&_Co "C. Hoare & Co") and [Guy's Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guy's_Hospital "Guy's Hospital") (1724) funded from the bequest of the wealthy merchant, [Thomas Guy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Guy "Thomas Guy"). Other hospitals sprang up in London and other British cities over the century, many paid for by private subscriptions. St. Bartholomew's in London was rebuilt in 1730, and the London Hospital opened in 1752.

These hospitals represented a turning point in the function of the institution; they began to evolve from being basic places of care for the sick to becoming centres of medical innovation and discovery and the principal place for the [education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_education "Medical education") and training of prospective practitioners. Some of the era's greatest [surgeons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surgeon "Surgeon") and doctors worked and passed on their knowledge at the hospitals.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-117) They also changed from being mere homes of refuge to being complex institutions for the provision of medicine and care for sick. The [Charité](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charit%C3%A9 "Charité") was founded in Berlin in 1710 by King [Frederick I of Prussia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_I_of_Prussia "Frederick I of Prussia") as a response to an outbreak of plague.

The concept of voluntary hospitals also spread to [Colonial America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonial_America "Colonial America"); the [Bellevue Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellevue_Hospital "Bellevue Hospital") opened in 1736, [Pennsylvania Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Hospital "Pennsylvania Hospital") in 1752, [New York Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Hospital "New York Hospital") in 1771, and [Massachusetts General Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_General_Hospital "Massachusetts General Hospital") in 1811. When the [Vienna General Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_General_Hospital "Vienna General Hospital") opened in 1784 (instantly becoming the world's largest hospital), physicians acquired a new facility that gradually developed into one of the most important research centres.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-118)

Another [Enlightenment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment "Age of Enlightenment") era charitable innovation was the dispensary; these would issue the poor with [medicines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicine "Medicine") free of charge. The London Dispensary opened its doors in 1696 as the first such clinic in the British Empire. The idea was slow to catch on until the 1770s, when many such organizations began to appear, including the [Public Dispensary of Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Dispensary_of_Edinburgh "Public Dispensary of Edinburgh") (1776), the [Metropolitan Dispensary and Charitable Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Dispensary_and_Charitable_Fund?action=edit&redlink=1 "Metropolitan Dispensary and Charitable Fund (page does not exist)") (1779) and the [Finsbury Dispensary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finsbury_Dispensary "Finsbury Dispensary") (1780). Dispensaries were also opened in New York 1771, Philadelphia 1786, and Boston 1796.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-119)

Across Europe medical schools still relied primarily on lectures and readings. In the final year, students would have limited clinical experience by following the professor through the wards. Laboratory work was uncommon, and [dissections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissection "Dissection") were rarely done because of legal restrictions on [cadavers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadaver "Cadaver"). Most schools were small, and only [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh"), [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland"), with 11,000 alumni, produced large numbers of graduates.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-120)[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-121)

## 19th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: 19th century")]

See also: [Category:Hospitals established in the 19th century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Hospitals_established_in_the_19th_century "Category:Hospitals established in the 19th century")

### United Kingdom

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: United Kingdom")]

English physician [Thomas Percival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Percival "Thomas Percival") (1740–1804) wrote a comprehensive system of medical conduct, _[Medical Ethics; or, a Code of Institutes and Precepts, Adapted to the Professional Conduct of Physicians and Surgeons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical\_Ethics;\_or,\_a\_Code\_of\_Institutes\_and\_Precepts,\_Adapted\_to\_the\_Professional\_Conduct\_of\_Physicians\_and\_Surgeons "Medical Ethics; or, a Code of Institutes and Precepts, Adapted to the Professional Conduct of Physicians and Surgeons")_ (1803) that set the standard for many textbooks.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-122)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/97/%27One_of_the_wards_in_the_hospital_at_Scutari%27._Wellcome_M0007724_-_restoration%2C_cropped.jpg/250px-%27One_of_the_wards_in_the_hospital_at_Scutari%27._Wellcome_M0007724_-_restoration%2C_cropped.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:'One_of_the_wards_in_the_hospital_at_Scutari'._Wellcome_M0007724_-_restoration,_cropped.jpg)

A ward of the hospital at [Scutari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%9Csk%C3%BCdar "Üsküdar") where [Florence Nightingale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_Nightingale "Florence Nightingale") worked and helped to restructure the modern hospital.

In the mid 19th century, hospitals and the medical profession became more professionalized, with a reorganization of hospital management along more bureaucratic and administrative lines. The [Apothecaries Act 1815](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apothecaries_Act_1815 "Apothecaries Act 1815") made it compulsory for medical students to practice for at least half a year at a hospital as part of their training.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-123) An example of this professionalization was the [Charing Cross Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charing_Cross_Hospital "Charing Cross Hospital"), set up in 1818 as the 'West London Infirmary and Dispensary' from funds provided by Dr. [Benjamin Golding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Golding "Benjamin Golding"). By 1821 it was treating nearly 10,000 patients a year, and it was relocated to larger quarters near [Charing Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charing_Cross "Charing Cross") in the heart of London. Its [Charing Cross Hospital Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charing_Cross_Hospital_Medical_School "Charing Cross Hospital Medical School") opened in 1822. It expanded several times and 1866 added a professional nursing staff.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-124)

[Florence Nightingale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_Nightingale "Florence Nightingale") pioneered the modern profession of [nursing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nursing "Nursing") during the [Crimean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimean_War "Crimean War") when she set an example of compassion, commitment to patient care and diligent and thoughtful hospital administration. The first official nurses' training programme, the Nightingale School for Nurses, was opened in 1860, with the mission of training nurses to work in hospitals, to work with the poor and to teach.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-125)

Nightingale was instrumental in reforming the nature of the hospital, by improving [sanitation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanitation "Sanitation") standards and changing the image of the hospital from a place the sick would go to die, to an institution devoted to recuperation and healing. She also emphasized the importance of [statistical measurement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics "Statistics") for determining the success rate of a given intervention and pushed for [administrative reform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_administration "Public administration") at hospitals.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-126)

The [National Health Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Health_Service "National Health Service"), the principal provider of health care in Britain, was founded in 1948, and took control of nearly all the hospitals.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-127)

### Continental Europe

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Continental Europe")]

During the middle of the 19th century, the [Second Viennese Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_General_Hospital "Vienna General Hospital") emerged with the contributions of physicians such as [Carl Freiherr von Rokitansky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Freiherr_von_Rokitansky "Carl Freiherr von Rokitansky"), [Josef Škoda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josef_%C5%A0koda "Josef Škoda"), [Ferdinand Ritter von Hebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Ritter_von_Hebra "Ferdinand Ritter von Hebra"), and [Ignaz Philipp Semmelweis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignaz_Philipp_Semmelweis "Ignaz Philipp Semmelweis"). Basic medical science expanded and specialization advanced. Furthermore, the first dermatology, eye, as well as ear, nose, and throat clinics in the world were founded in [Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna "Vienna").[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-128)

In Rome, where hospitality was highly patrimonial thanks to a long tradition of bequests and substantial donations (_[Spedalità romane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spedalit%C3%A0\_romane?action=edit&redlink=1 "Spedalità romane (page does not exist)")_), with a royal decree in [1896](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1896 "1896") the vast hospital patrimony was centralized in a single body: the [Pio Istituto di Santo Spirito and Ospedali Riuniti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pio_Istituto_di_Santo_Spirito_and_Ospedali_Riuniti?action=edit&redlink=1 "Pio Istituto di Santo Spirito and Ospedali Riuniti (page does not exist)"), which thus became the largest in Europe.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-129)

By the late 19th century, the modern hospital was beginning to take shape with a proliferation of a variety of public and private hospital systems. By the 1870s, hospitals had more than tripled their original average intake of 3,000 patients. In [continental Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Europe "Continental Europe") the new hospitals generally were built and run from [public funds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_fund "Public fund").

### France

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: France")]

Nursing was professionalized in France by the turn of the 20th century. At that time, the country's 1,500 hospitals were operated by 15,000 [nuns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nun "Nun") representing over 200 [religious orders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_order "Religious order"). Government policy after 1900 was to [secularize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secularism "Secularism") public institutions, and diminish the role the [Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church"). This political goal came in conflict with the need to maintain better quality of medical care in antiquated facilities. New government-operated nursing schools turned out nonreligious nurses who were slated for supervisory roles. During the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_World_War "First World War"), an outpouring of [patriotic volunteers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriotism "Patriotism") brought large numbers of untrained middle-class women into the military hospitals. They left when the war ended but the long-term effect was to heighten the prestige of nursing. In 1922 the government issued a national diploma for nursing.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-130)

At the turn of the 19th century, Paris medicine played a significant role in shaping clinical medicine. New emphasis on physically examining the body led to methods such as [percussion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percussion_(medicine) "Percussion (medicine)"), inspection, [palpation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palpation "Palpation"), [auscultation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auscultation "Auscultation"), and [autopsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autopsy "Autopsy").[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-:0-131) The situation in Paris was particularly unique due to the fact that there was a very large concentration of medical professionals in a very small setting allowing for a large flow of ideas and the spread of innovation.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-:0-131) One of the innovations to come out of the Paris hospital setting was [Laennec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Laennec "René Laennec")'s [stethoscope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stethoscope "Stethoscope"). Weiner states that the widespread acceptance of the stethoscope would likely not have happened in any other setting, and the setting allowed for Laennec to pass on this technology to the eager medical community that had gathered there. This invention also brought even more attention to the Paris scene.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-:0-131)

Before the start of the 19th century, there were many problems existing within the French medical system. These problems were outlined by many seeking to reform hospitals including a contemporary surgeon Jacques Tenon in his book _Memoirs on Paris Hospitals_. Some of the problems Tenon drew attention to were the lack of space, the inability to separate patients based on the type of illness (including those that were contagious), and general sanitation problems.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-132) Additionally, the secular revolution led to the nationalization of hospitals previously owned by the Catholic Church and led to a call for a hospital reform which actually pushed for the deinstitutionalization of medicine.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-:1-133) This contributed to the state of disarray Paris hospitals soon fell into which ultimately called for the establishment of a new hospital system outlined in the law of 1794. The law of 1794 played a significant part in revolutionizing Paris Medicine because it aimed to address some of the problems facing Paris Hospitals of the time.

First, the law of 1794 created three new schools in Paris, Montpellier, and Strasbourg due to the lack of medical professionals available to treat a growing French army. It also gave physicians and surgeons equal status in the hospital environment, whereas previously physicians were regarded as intellectually superior.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-:1-133) This led to the integration of surgery into traditional medical education contributing to a new breed of doctors that focused on [pathology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pathology "Pathology"), [anatomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatomy "Anatomy") and diagnosis. The new focus on anatomy was further facilitated by this law because it ensured that medical students had enough bodies to dissect.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-:1-133) Additionally, pathological education was furthered by the increased use of autopsies to determine a patient's cause of death.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-:0-131) Lastly, the law of 1794 allocated funds for full-time salaried teachers in hospitals, as well as creating scholarships for medical students.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-:1-133) Overall, the law of 1794 contributed to the shift of medical teaching away from theory and towards practice and experience, all within a hospital setting. Hospitals became a center for learning and development of medical techniques, which was a departure from the previous notion of a hospital as an area that accepted people who needed help of any kind, ill or not.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-134) This shift was consistent with much of the philosophy of the time, particularly the ideas of [John Locke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Locke "John Locke") who preached that observation using ones senses was the best way to analyze and understand a phenomenon.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-:1-133)[Foucalt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_Foucault "Michel Foucault"), however, criticized this shift in his book _[The Birth of the Clinic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Birth\_of\_the\_Clinic "The Birth of the Clinic"),_ stating that this shift took attention away from the patient and objectified patients, ultimately resulting in a loss of the patient's narrative. He argued that from this point forward, in the eyes of doctors, patients lost their humanity and became more like objects for inspection and examination.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-135)

The next advancement in Paris medicine came with the creation of an examination system, that after 1803, was required for the licensing of all medical professions creating a uniform and centralized system of licensing.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-:1-133) This law also created another class of health professionals, mostly for those living outside of cities, who did not have to go through the licensing process but instead went through a simpler and shorter training process.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-:1-133)

Another area influenced by Paris hospitals was the development of specialties. The structure of a Paris hospital allowed physicians more freedom to pursue interests as well as providing the necessary resources.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-:0-131) An example of a physician who used this flexibility to conduct research is [Phillipe Pinel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippe_Pinel "Philippe Pinel") who conducted a four-year study on the hospitalization and treatment of mentally-ill women within the [Salpêtriére](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piti%C3%A9-Salp%C3%AAtri%C3%A8re_Hospital "Pitié-Salpêtrière Hospital") hospital. This was the first study ever done of this magnitude by a physician, and the Pinel was the first to realize that patients dealing with similar illnesses could be group together, compared, and classified.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-:0-131)

### Protestant hospitals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Protestant hospitals")]

Main article: [deaconess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deaconess "Deaconess")

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/Diacones_Kerk_Engeland.jpg/250px-Diacones_Kerk_Engeland.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Diacones_Kerk_Engeland.jpg)

[Elizabeth Catherine Ferard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Ferard "Elizabeth Ferard"), first deaconess of the [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

The [Protestant churches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_church "Protestant church") reentered the health field in the 19th century, especially with the establishment of orders of women, called [deaconesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deaconess "Deaconess") who dedicated themselves to nursing services. This movement began in Germany in 1836 when [Theodor Fliedner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodor_Fliedner "Theodor Fliedner") and his wife opened the first deaconess motherhouse in [Kaiserswerth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaiserswerth "Kaiserswerth") on the Rhine. It became a model, and within half a century there were over 5,000 deaconesses in Europe. Lutheran minister [William Passavant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Passavant "William Passavant") in 1849 brought the first four deaconesses to Pittsburgh, in the United States, after visiting Kaiserswerth. They worked at the Pittsburgh Infirmary (now Passavant Hospital).[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-136)

The [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England") named its first deaconess in 1862. The North London Deaconess Institution trained deaconesses for other dioceses and some served overseas.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-137)

### China

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: China")]

See also: [Chinese medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_medicine "Chinese medicine")

Traditionally, Chinese medicine relied on small private clinics and individual healers until the middle of the 18th century when missionary hospitals operated by western churches were first established in China. In 1870, the [Tung Wah Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tung_Wah_Hospital "Tung Wah Hospital") became the first hospital to offer [Traditional Chinese Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_Chinese_Medicine "Traditional Chinese Medicine"). After the cultural revolution in 1949, most Chinese hospitals became public.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-Dudovskiy-138)[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-Tungwah-139)

### United States

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: United States")]

Further information: [History of public health in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_public_health_in_the_United_States "History of public health in the United States")

American hospitals in the 19th century were largely designed for poor people in the larger cities. There were no paying patients. Very small proprietary hospitals were operated by practicing physicians and surgeons to take care of their own paying patients in better facilities than the charity hospitals offered. By the 1840s, the major religious denominations, especially the Catholics and Methodists, began opening hospitals in major cities. The South had small hospitals in its few cities. In the rich plantation areas, slave owners hired physicians to keep their slaves in working shape. In the poor white areas there were few doctors and very few hospitals.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-140)

In the U.S., the number of hospitals reached 4400 in 1910, when they provided 420,000 beds.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-141) These were operated by city, state and federal agencies, by churches, by stand-alone non-profits, and by [for-profit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For-profit_hospital "For-profit hospital") enterprises. [Non-profit hospitals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-profit_hospital "Non-profit hospital") were supplemented by large [public hospitals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_hospital "Public hospital") in major cities and research hospitals often affiliated with a medical school. The largest public hospital system in America is the [New York City Health and Hospitals Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Health_and_Hospitals_Corporation "New York City Health and Hospitals Corporation"), which includes [Bellevue Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellevue_Hospital "Bellevue Hospital"), the oldest U.S. hospital, affiliated with [New York University Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_University_Medical_School "New York University Medical School").

#### New York City

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: New York City")]

According to historian [Mike Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Wallace_(historian) "Mike Wallace (historian)"), in the early 20th century, a significant shift occurred in New York City's private hospitals. In 1911 came the partnership of [Presbyterian Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Hospital_(New_York_City) "Presbyterian Hospital (New York City)") with [Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University_College_of_Physicians_and_Surgeons "Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons"), In 1912 [New York Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weill_Cornell_Medical_Center "Weill Cornell Medical Center") forged its own alliance with [Cornell University Medical College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornell_University_Medical_School "Cornell University Medical School").[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-142) These collaborations marked a pivot towards medical education and scientific research, fundamentally altering how these institutions operated and who they served. Previously, 19th-century religious and charitable hospitals functioned much like public ones, primarily caring for the sick poor. Their focus was on care rather than cures, with little integration of medical practice. Wallace argues that the emergence of scientific medicine changed everything. Improved antiseptic practices made hospitals the ideal location for surgery, as medical advancements rendered home operations increasingly difficult. Hospitals offered doctors crucial technical resources and supported their professional independence. They also employed trained assistants, often women, who helped physicians efficiently treat more patients. This evolution solidified hospitals as central hubs for medical practice. Despite receiving funding from corporate philanthropists for new facilities, hospitals faced escalating operational costs. To remain viable, they began targeting wealthier patients, who had previously only sought hospital care in emergencies. To attract this new clientele, hospital boards redesigned their institutions to mimic luxury hotels. For example, [Roosevelt Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Sinai_West "Mount Sinai West") marketed its private patients' pavilion as a refined choice for individuals with "the most cultivated tastes."[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-143)

#### Chicago

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Chicago")]

Further information: [History of public health in Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_public_health_in_Chicago "History of public health in Chicago")

The history of hospitals in Chicago is rich with innovation, diversity, and rapid growth, reflecting the city's development as a major medical center.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-144)[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-145) Before the emergence of modern hospitals, Chicago relied on a neighborhood based dispensary system to provide medical help for poor people without charge.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-146)

Before the 1870s, hospitals had a bad reputation. Poor people went there to die, even those who were not fatally ill when they arrived. Bad sanitation on the part of doctors spread disease inside the hospital. Finally.the discovery of the germ theory of disease produced an immediate transition to concerns with sanitation. and cleanliness.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-147) After the Great Fire of 1871, Chicago's hospital system grew rapidly in response to the city's burgeoning population. The city's first hospital was built in 1843 in response to epidemic fears. Vaccination programs for the poor began in 1848. Specialized facilities were created for specific health crises, such as smallpox and cholera. The expansion was characterized by steady increases of bed capacity to meet growing demand; specialization to serve specific communities and medical needs; and the development of new facilities and technologies.

In 1927 and 1928—years of peak prosperity—numerous hospitals expanded or were newly built, including Mercy Hospital (now part of [Insight Hospital and Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insight_Hospital_and_Medical_Center "Insight Hospital and Medical Center")), Passavant Memorial Hospital (now part of [Northwestern Memorial Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwestern_Memorial_Hospital "Northwestern Memorial Hospital"), and Edgewater Hospital. In 1916 the University of Chicago obtained funding for. an independent academic medical school effort with a teaching hospital. The facility opened in 1927 and is now the [Pritzker School of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pritzker_School_of_Medicine "Pritzker School of Medicine").[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-148)

The late 20th century saw significant changes in hospital operations and funding, By 1950, Chicago had 84 hospitals serving a population of 3.6 million. They increasingly focused on attracting paying patients with improved amenities and services.[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-149) Since 1965 [Medicare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_(United_States) "Medicare (United States)") and [Medicaid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicaid "Medicaid") and other federal programs dramatically expanded spending on health nationwide. As the stockyards closed and old manufacturing industries faded away, health spending increasingly dominated the Chicago economy.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-150)

#### Religious hospitals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Religious hospitals")]

All the major denominations built hospitals; the 541 Catholic ones (in 1915) were staffed primarily by unpaid nuns. The others sometimes had a small cadre of [deaconesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deaconesses "Deaconesses") as staff.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-151) The American [Methodists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodist "Methodist") made medical services a priority from the 1850s. They began opening charitable institutions such as orphanages and old people's homes. In the 1880s, Methodists began opening hospitals in the United States, which served people of all religious beliefs. By 1895, 13 hospitals were in operation in major cities.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-152)

In the 1840s–1880s era, Catholics in Philadelphia founded two hospitals, for the Irish and German Catholics. They depended on revenues from the paying sick, and became important health and welfare institutions in the Catholic community.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-153) By 1900 the Catholics had set up hospitals in most major cities. In New York the Dominicans, Franciscans, Sisters of Charity, and other orders set up hospitals to care primarily for their own ethnic group. By the 1920s they were serving everyone in the neighborhood.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-154) In smaller cities too the Catholics set up hospitals, such as St. Patrick Hospital in [Missoula, Montana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missoula,_Montana "Missoula, Montana"). The Sisters of Providence opened it in 1873. It was in part funded by the county contract to care for the poor, and also operated a day school and a boarding school. The nuns provided nursing care especially for infectious diseases and traumatic injuries among the young, heavily male clientele. They also proselytized the patients to attract converts and restore lapsed Catholics back into the Church. They built a larger hospital in 1890.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-155) Catholic hospitals were largely staffed by Catholic orders of nuns, and nursing students, until the population of nuns dropped sharply after the 1960s. The Catholic Hospital Association formed in 1915.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-156)[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-157)

## Integration of new technology and advancements

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Integration of new technology and advancements")]

### Anesthetics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_hospitals&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Anesthetics")]

A major change to procedures in the medical field was the introduction of [anesthetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anesthetic "Anesthetic") used to put patients to sleep.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-:03-158) While the use of anesthetics was first introduced in the 19th century, it became a favorable and widely used practice due to its ability to incapacitate a patient and make operations easier and less painful.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-:03-158) This, in turn, made operations such as amputations less fatal, because patients would stay still as well as not be in shock and lose less blood while being operated on.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_hospitals#cite_note-:03-158)

Chapter 4

Gazetteer of Towns and Villages in County Cork

This chapter contains the details on circa 200 different settlements throughout the county of

fully in Irish (the English translations are included as an appendix in the back of  the book).

In  relation  to  each  settlement,  the  meaning  behind  the  location’s  name  is  provided. While  some
of  these names are open to interpretation, this publication provides the most generally accepted
translation from available published sources – note, however, that these are not meant in any way
to  be  definitive.  Each  entry  also  includes  coordinates  indicating  the  location  of  each  settlement
(coordinates are provided in order of  Latitude, Longitude, then X and Y Coordinates) and recent
and past population figures are also provided, where such detail is available.

The description of  each settlement starts with a general location, with distance from the nearest
large  population  centre  provided,  as  well  as  its  topographical  setting.  Each  entry  also  generally
discusses the historical origin of  the settlement; outlines the main historic buildings that can
be  seen  today  and  provides  general  remarks  about  its  architecture  and  streetscape.  Where
completed  for  the  relevant  town(s),  the  text  from  Cork  County  Council’s  Historic  Town  Maps,  is
used as the entry.

Read on to learn about the places we call home, and how they became the places that we know
in the first instance.

Adrigole- Eadargóil  Placename Meaning: (between creeks)
Location Coordinates:  51.694648  -9.7294663  081104  050499

Adrigole  is  a  village  on  the  southern  shore  of  the  Beara  Peninsula,  c.  13.5  kilometres  east  of
Castletownberehaven, on the route of  the Wild Atlantic Way.

This is a scattered settlement, arrayed
along the north bank of  the Adrigole River
and the north shore of  Adrigole Bay, west
of  Adrigole  Bridge.  The  1842  OS  map
marks a Metal Foundry (in ruins) and an
Old Furnace a short distance west of  the
bridge.  According  to  McCracken  (1957,
127)  there  was  a  large  ironworks  here  in
the 17th and 18th centuries. All that survives
now is a featureless structure, but the area
around  it  is  strewn  with  slag  and  vitrified
stone.  From  the  early  17th century, the
native oak woods of  the peninsula were
systematically felled to produce charcoal  Adrigole Harbour. Image by Mick Garratt on geography.org.uk,
for use in the smelting of  iron.  sourced via OpenVerse.

45

[PDF page 2]
Also,  in  this  area  on  the  1842  map,  is  a  Church  of  Ireland  church  and  beside  it  Adrigole  school
house;  a  police  station  and  Adrigole  Parsonage.  The  church  was  described  by  Lewis  (1837,
vol.  2,  59)  as  a  “small  edifice  with  low  square  tower...built  1809”. There is no trace now of  either
the  church  or  the  school.  The  police  barracks  was  replaced  in  the  mid-20th century by a Garda
barracks.

The old Adrigole Telegraph Office, c. 1920. Image sourced from Creative Commons.

By  the  late  19th  century,  a  national  school  had  been  built  north  of  the  bridge  and  a  hotel  to
west of  it. The national school has been replaced by a modern school, but the hotel is still there,
a  three-storey  roadside  building.  On  the  north  side  of  the  bridge  is  the  former  post  office  and
telegraph office, now converted into a private residence.

Aghabullouge- Achadh  Bolg  Placename Meaning: field of  the swelling
Location Coordinates:51.944894  -8.807679  077246  144517

A village in Mid Cork, c. 4.5 kilometres north-north-west of  Coachford.

Aghabullogue is a shifted settlement, as the ancient settlement was in the vicinity of  the old
graveyard that lies c. 1 kilometre north-north-west of  the current village. That graveyard is the site
of  a  monastery  founded  by  St.  Eolaing  (Olan).  It  is  one  of  the  few  Cork  foundations  mentioned
in  the  early  9th  century  Martyrology  of  Tallaght,  indicating  it  was  an  important  foundation
(MacCotter, 2013, 39).

Its  antiquity  as  a  place  of  importance  is  emphasized  by  the  survival  of  two  ogham  stones  in
the  graveyard  and  a  third  nearby  at  St.  Olan’s  holy  well.  St.  Olan’s  ogham  stone  stands  in  the
graveyard; it had a moveable cap of  a semi-globular shape (now affixed to the top of  the stone),
known  as  the  Coppeen  Olan,  St.  Olan’s  Cap,  and  local  tradition  holds  that  it  was  much  sought
after  for  female  illness  and  ailments  as  well  as  a  cure  for  headaches!  According  to  MacCotter
(2013,  40)  a  large  village  had  existed  around  the  old  graveyard,  but  was  destroyed  during  the

Church of  Ireland built a parish church in the old graveyard, which was replaced by a new church
in  1838.  The  sod-covered  remains  of  the  earlier  church  and  a  ruined  gable  of  the  latter  can  still
be seen in the graveyard.

As the Protestant population declined through the 19th century, the focus of  settlement shifted to
the  vicinity  of  the  Catholic  church  of  St.  John’s,  built  in  1828,  a  kilometre  to  the  south  of  the  old

46

[PDF page 3]
graveyard. This  today  is  the  location  of  Aghabullogue  village  -  a  thin  scattering  of  houses,  most
of  them modern. The 1840’s map shows a long rectangular schoolhouse on the south side of  the
churchyard, as shown in the 1900’s postcard (pictured). This school was replaced by the present
school.

Aghabullogue village c. 1900s, with St. John’s Catholic church on right, partly hidden behind the old schoolhouse

One  of  the  most  interesting  and  accessible  holy  wells  in  the  county  is  St.  Olan’s  Well,  c.  0.5
kilometres north-east of  the old graveyard. The well is covered by a corbeled drystone dome and
beside it stands a tall ogham stone discovered nearby, when a local corn mill was demolished.
Rounds are made at the well on St. Olan’s feast day, 5th September.

St. Olan’s Cap and Ogham Stone, located in

A twin village (Upper Aghada and Lower Aghada) on the eastern shore of  Cork Harbour, between
Whitegate and Rostellan. Aghada Lower is on the shoreline, Aghada Upper is on higher ground,
inland.

Aghada was created by the Normans, early in their conquest of  East Cork. Their dedication of  the
medieval  parish  church  to  St.  Erasmus,  the  patron  saint  of  sailors,  indicates  the  maritime  nature
of  the  settlement,  though  the  location  of  the  church  was  on  high  ground  c.  1  kilometre  south  of
the  shoreline  of  Cork  Harbour. This  dedication  to  St.  Erasmus  continues  today  with  the  Catholic
church  in  the  village.  With  the  building  of  a  fine  stone  pier  on  the  shoreline  in  the  early  19th
century, it became inevitable that Aghada would develop as a twin village, one part adjacent to
the pier (Lower) and the second, at the older parish centre to the south (Upper).

Upper Aghada, on the higher ground, has two short streets extending north-east and south-west
from an open area that was probably once a market place. The ruin of  a late medieval parish
church  sits  in  the  old  graveyard  on  the  west  side  of  the  village.  A  Church  of  Ireland  church  was
built  in  1815  a  short  distance  outside  the  village  to  the  west;  it  was  converted  to  a  Presbyterian
church in 1925. It is a rectangular building with a bell tower on its west gable. The 19th century St.
Erasmus Catholic church has been demolished apart from its belltower, which stands overlooking
the  village  street;  a  new  church  was  built  behind  it  in  1987. The  village  retains  some  of  the  one-
storey  three-bay  terraced  houses  that  lined  the  short  street  in  the  19th century, though all have
been modernised. There are two fine traditional shopfronts, both with the family name Walsh on
their fascia.

The 1842 OS map shows two 2-storey terraces in Aghada Lower as the only housing - both have
been  partially  modified  over  time  but  there  is  a  more  intact  terrace  of  similar  houses  a  short
distance  along  the  shore  road  to  the  east.  The  limestone  pier  is  an  impressive  example  of  mid-
19th century marine construction.

Traditional shop fronts in Upper Aghada.

48

[PDF page 5]
Aghern- Áth  Cairn Placename Meaning:the ford of  the cairn
Location Coordinates:  52.086679  -8.152158  092724  189620

A small crossroads village on the main road from Rathcormac to
Tallow (R628), on the south side of  a bridge, over the River Bride.

As its name suggests, this settlement owes its origin to a ford
across  the  Bride.  The  ford  is  marked  on  the  1842  OS  map,
just  east  of  the  bridge;  the  bridge  being  an  impressive  triple-
arched  structure,  erected  in  1826.  The  old  parish  church  of
Athcarryng  (Ahern)  was  dedicated  to  St.  Columba  (Colmcille),
which  MacCotter  (2013,  144)  thinks  makes  it  very  ancient;  the
site is now occupied by a Church of  Ireland church, built in 1817.
The  church  is  rectangular  in  plan  with  a  3-storey  bell  tower  on
its west gable. The castle, like the church, is on the north side
of  the river, and consists of  two towers linked by a wall. Though
much reduced in size, the ruin has 13th and 15th century features.
It  stands  on  the  south  side  of  Aghern  House,  a  2-storey  country
house built in the mid-18th century.  Aghern Church of Ireland church.
Image courtesy of NIAH.
Whilst  the  medieval  focus  was  on  the  north  side  of  the  river,  the
19th century village moved south to where the road crossing the
bridge  meets  the  main  Rathcormac-Tallow  road.  According  to  Lewis  (1837,  vol.  1,  18)  the  road
crossing  the  bridge  was  “the  mail  car  road  from  Rathcormac  to  Castle  Martyr”; it is possible that
the crossroads was a stop for the coach - there is a pub here now. Apart from a small number of
houses  at  the  crossroads,  the  settlement  was  defined  in  the  mid-19th century by several service
buildings stretched along the road to the west. These were a forge, a police barracks, a school,
and a sessions house.

According  to  Lewis  (ibid.)  petty  sessions,  minor  court  proceedings,  were  held  here  on  the  first
Thursday of  each month. None of  these buildings survive and the village never evolved beyond
a  crossroads  settlement.  Today,  on  the  north-east  corner  of  the  crossroads,  is  an  example  of  a
1-storey thatched cottage once typical of  such villages - it now has a corrugated iron roof.

1842 OS map of Aghern, showing petty session house, schoolhouse, police barracks, Aghern bridge and ford, Aghern
house with castle adjacent, and the Church of Ireland church and graveyard

49

[PDF page 6]
Aghyohil- Achadh  EochaillePlacename Meaning: field of  the yew wood
Location Coordinates:  51.710124  -8.892093  051196  138393

A crossroads village in West Cork, located roughly half-way between Enniskean and Ballinascarty.

Allihies-  Ailichí  Placename Meaning: cliff  fields
Location Coordinates: 51.641369  -10.04444  045150  58542

A village at the western end of  the Beara Peninsula, surrounded by the rugged hilly landscape of
the Slieve Miskish Mountains, c. 9.3 kilometres west of  Castletownberehaven.

The mining for copper ore began here in 1812 when John Puxley, whose ancestors were smugglers
from  West  Cork,  founded  the  Allihies  Mining  Company.  Through  skilful  management,  Puxley
established a thriving industry, which at its height in the 1830s and 1840s, employed over 1,000
people and produced some 3,000 tons of  copper ore each year. Many of  the miners were Cornish
and  the  remains  of  their  settlement  can  still  be  seen  north  of  the  present  village.  After  Puxley’s
death  in  1856,  the  mining  began  a  slow  decline  and  when  the  Berehaven  Mining  Company  was
wound-up in 1884, that effectively was the end of  the enterprise. Relations between the Cornish
miners and the natives were never cordial and once the
mines closed, most of  them emigrated to America.

Drainage of  the mines was always a problem and two of
the surviving structures are pump houses, with their tall,
elegant  chimney  stacks,  one  at  Mountain  Mine  and  the
other  at  Coom  Mine  (see  Industrial  Heritage  of  County
Cork, Exemplar 1, 110-112).

The  village  itself  is  shown  on  the  1842  OS  map,  as  a
scattering of  buildings stretching from the old medieval
parish church of  Kilnamanagh at the southern end, to the
Mountain  Mine  complex  at  the  far  end,  but  not  holding  a
streetline. The only service buildings marked on the map
are a police barracks and a post office.

By 1900, the village proper has taken shape with a winding
street running north from the Protestant church, past the
school and Catholic church as far north as a constabulary
barracks.  The  Protestant  church,  built  in  1845,  has  been
Mountain Mine pump house on hillside  converted  into  the  Allihies  Copper  Mine  Museum  (see
overlooking Allihies village.  Heritage Artefacts of  County Cork, 285-286).

The  Catholic  church  of  St.  Michael  is  a  mid-19th century
plain  neo-Gothic  rectangular  building.  The  streetline,  composed  mostly  of  2-storey  houses,  is
not continuous but composed of  several short terraces with individual houses and open spaces
in  between.  In  recent  times,  the  village  streetscape  is  noted  for  the  striking  vivid  colour  of  its
buildings.

Ardfield- Árd Ó bhFicheallaigh Placename Meaning: the high ground of  the O’Fehillys
Location Coordinates:  51.566915  -8.909095  035279  137020

A  village  in  West  Cork,  c.  6.2  kilometres  south  of  Clonakilty,  in  an  elevated  location  overlooking
Galley Head and the coastline to the south.

Ardfield  is  an  example  of  a  twin  village  where  two  crossroads,  c.  0.7  kilometres  apart,  are  the
focus of  settlement and share the same name. Neither includes the old medieval church site, that
lies a short distance to the south in the countryside, so the focus of  settlement has shifted north
towards these crossroads in the post-medieval period.

The  focus  of  the  northern  most  crossroads  is  St.  James’s  Catholic  church. This  is  a T-plan  church
built  in  1832,  in  a  plain  but  confident  neo-Gothic  style.  The  interior  retains  its  19th century
appearance and has a notable open-truss roof  dated to 1913. Immediately west of  the church, a
national school is depicted on the OS map. This is now converted into a private dwelling but the
stone plaque on its gable is inscribed “Scoil Náisiúnta/An Aird/1832.”

The second crossroads to the south had just a couple of  buildings in 1840 but by 1900 there was
a  post  office  here  and  the  name  Ardfield  is  affixed  to  this  cluster  rather  than  to  the  crossroads
with the church and school further north. At both crossroads are some 2-storey stone-built gable-
ended houses of  a modest, but attractive, appearance.

Ardfield National School, with St. James church in background, dated 1832

Near  the  village  is  St.  James’  holy  well.  James  is  associated  with  Santiago  de  Compostella  in
northern Spain, still the destination of  a world-famous camino or pilgrimage. This pilgrimage was
also  undertaken  from  Ireland  in  medieval  times  and  must  have  had  some  link  to Ardfield  for  the
holy well and the Catholic church to have this dedication.

A village on the north coast of  the Beara Peninsula, c. 9.2 kilometres north of  Castletownberehaven.
The  1842  OS  map  shows  a  bridge  here,  Slieve  Bridge,  over  the  Owenagappul  River,  at  a
crossroads,  but  without  any  building  in  its  vicinity.  By  the  late  19th century, a small village had
developed with a single straight street, running north from a small bridge over the river. The
village is located between a Catholic church a short distance to the north and a carding mill to the
south, so this is a combination of  a chapel village, a crossroads village, and a mill village.

The church is cruciform in plan and late-19th century in appearance. At the mill, wool was prepared
by a carding machine for spinning; this industry is not surprising in an area renowned for its
sheep farming. The mill is a 1-storey building with a wheel pit on its south gable where power was
taken from the river; it is now used as a farm building.

The  street  comprises  mostly  of  two-storey  houses,  many  colourfully  painted  in  the  fashion  of
villages at this end of  the Beara Peninsula.

A village on the west bank of  the Bandon River, c. 7.4 kilometres west of  Kinsale.

where it meets the top of  Ballinadee Creek, an inlet of  the Bandon River. The river was important
as it provided power for a large corn mill that still stands on the north bank of  the river close to
the  bridge;  it  is  4-storeys  high,  built  around  1800,  enlarged  in  1836,  and  is  now  used  as  a  farm
building. According  to  Lewis,  it  was  ‘a  large  flour  mill  of  great  power,  which  was  much  improved
in  1836.’  Close  to  the  bridge  on  the  creek,  the  1842  OS  map  shows  three  small  boat  quays.
According  to  Lewis  (1837,  vol.  1,  107),  this  is  where  “great  quantities  of  sea  sand  for  manure  are
landed for the supply of  the adjacent parishes.”

A town on the south bank of  the River Lee, c. 8 kilometres west of  the city centre, gradually being
engulfed by the westward expansion of  the city.

In medieval times, the Ballincollig area was borderland between the Gaelic west and the Norman
east,  as  the  Mac  Carthys  began  to  push  east  along  the  Lee  Valley  against  the  colonists.  By  the
14th century, the Barrets, a family of  Norman origin, had carved out a territory for themselves in
this borderland; this extended further south than the later Barret ’s Barony which does not include
Ballincollig.  In  1468  the  Barrets  extended  their  territory  by  purchasing  Ballincollig  from  Robert
Cole/Coll. The castle here then became their chief  residence. The ruin of  Ballincollig Castle stands
on a rocky outcrop, c. 1.2 kilometres south-west of  the town (see Heritage Castles of  County Cork,
Exemplar 7, 75-77), the castle itself  dating to the end of  the 14th century.

The  modern  village  of  Ballincollig  owes  its  origin  to  the  development  in  1794  of  gunpowder
mills  along  the  south  bank  of  the  River  Lee  (see  Industrial  Heritage  of  County  Cork,  Exemplar
21,  171-174). This  was  established  by  two  Cork  merchants,  Charles  Leslie  and  John Travers,  but
was  taken  over  by  the  British  Army  in  1805  to  supply  ammunition  during  the  Napoleonic  Wars.
The  complex  originally  stretched  over  53  hectares  (130  acres)  but  was  greatly  expanded  by  the
Board  of  Ordnance  between  1806  and  1815  to  cover  175  hectares  (430  acres).  A  large  artillery
barracks  was  built  in  1810,  fronting  onto  the  road  west  from  Cork,  to  enhance  the  site’s  security,
and the entire area of  the mills and the barracks was enclosed by a high stone wall, long sections
of  which  survive  along  the  western  side  of  the  complex.  The  barracks  was  burnt  by  the  IRA  in
1922  during  the  Civil  War.  It  was  later  restored  as  an  Irish  Army  barracks,  but  this  was  closed  in
1998. The gunpowder mills was purchased by Cork County Council in 1974, who restored some
of  the mill buildings and structures and established the area as a public park; the park is now
owned and maintained by Cork City Council. Ballincollig Gunpowder Mills is the largest industrial
archaeological site in the country.

station house remains located south of  the main road between the two villages. The bridge is
a  fine  example  of  an  18th century bridge, which was later widened on the downstream side to

A village in North Cork, c. 7 kilometres north-west of  Mallow.

The present village sits very close to, if  not on top, of  its medieval forbearer, judging by the
remains of  the medieval parish in the Church of  Ireland graveyard at the west end of  the village,
and the late medieval tower house, just north of  its eastern end. The tower house was built in
the 15th century by a branch of  the Barrys known as the Mac Roberts; the Barrys were of  Norman
origin and became one of  the chief  landowners in this part of  North Cork from the 13th century.

After  the  Cromwellian  confiscations  of  the  mid-17th century, the lands of  Ballyclough passed
to  the  Purdon  family,  who  lived  in  the  tower  house,  which  they  subsequently  converted  into  a
country  house.  In  1750,  Smith  described  Ballyclough  as  “a  pretty  village,  being  improved  by  the
late colonel Purdon”. Probably by then, the village had taken its shape, with a wide straight main
street, suggesting it is a planned village.

1842 OS Map, Ballyclough.

By  1842,  the  village  had  extended  north  and  south  from  the  western  end  of  the  main  street,
following the roads travelling in those directions. Just beyond the village to the north was the old
Catholic church - this was replaced in 1850 by the present church at the other end of  the village,
near  the  Fair  Green.  On  the  south  side,  the  street  extends  sharply  around  the  enclosing  wall  of
the  old  graveyard  and  ran  a  short  distance  towards  two  adjacent  corn  mills.  By  1900,  the  village
had  shrunk  somewhat  but  still  had  a  court  house,  a  dispensary,  a  post  office,  a  constabulary
barracks, a school, and a creamery.

appearance.  The  former  Church  of  Ireland  parish  church  stands  on  the  streetline  at  the  west
end  of  the  south  side  of  the  street;  it  has  been  converted  into  a  funeral  home.  It  was  built  in
the  1830s  on  a  rectangular  plan  with  a  bell  tower  on  its  west  gable;  a  chancel  was  added  in  the
1870s. The nave had three lancet windows but the central one has been replaced by a doorway.
The  graveyard  to  the  rear  has  two  important  18th  century  tombs.  A  square  mausoleum  of  the

a Latin inscription. The other is a classical monument of  the Longfield family, erected in 1765.

The Catholic church, dedicated to St. John the Baptist, is rectangular in plan, the side walls having
seven lancet windows with ogee arched heads. The east window has tracery and stained glass. It
stands in an elevated position overlooking the Mallow Road, south-east of  the village itself. Close
to the church, where the creamery once stood, is a stone sculpture of  a milk churn being emptied
by two men, a commemoration of  the once everyday scene at creameries in County Cork.

Ballydehob  is  a  coastal  village  in  West  Cork,  located  at  the  junction  of  the  Skibbereen-Bantry
Road (N71) with the Skibbereen-Schull Road (R592), c. 13 kilometres west of  Skibbereen.

In the early 17th century, Richard Boyle, the Earl of  Cork, established the Manor of  Ballydehob from
lands  he  purchased  from  the  Slíocht  Taidhg,  an  offshoot  branch  of  the  O  Mahonys  (Maccarthy-
Morrogh 1986, 160-161). Boyle’s intention would be to establish a village of  settlers from England,
probably  fishermen,  to  exploit  the  pilchard  fisheries  then  flourishing  along  the West  Cork  coast.
Whatever  the  nature  of  this  settlement,  it  doesn’t  seem  to  have  flourished  because  Smith,  in  his
History of  Cork (1750, vol. 2, 274), makes no mention of  Ballydehob.

Ballydehob road bridge

But  its  fortune  changed  in  the  early  19th century, with the construction of a new road from
Skibbereen  to  Crookhaven,  with  a  branch  to  Bantry  from  Ballydehob  (O’Keeffe  1980,  62-63).  A
fine  three  arched  road  bridge  was  built  to  carry  the  road  over  the  head  of  Ballydehob  Bay.  The
junction is on the west side of  the bridge, and this is where the village is located. The road scheme
was  completed  in  1826  and  by  1831,  the  village  had  grown  to  100  houses  and  a  population  of
600  (Lewis  1837,  vol.  1,  132).  In  1886,  the  West  Carbery Tramways  and  Light  Railways  Company,
opened  a  line  from  Skibbereen  to  Schull  with  a  station  at  Ballydehob,  though  the  station  was
inconveniently located a distance from the village on the east side of  the bridge. The line closed
in 1947 but its twelve-arch viaduct across the tidal inlet remains an important heritage landmark.
The viaduct is now part of  a public footpath and can be walked across.

narrow  street  is  lined  by  terraces  of  two-  and  three-storey  houses  that  give  a  strong  early-19th
century  character  to  the  street.  The  street  also  has  a  selection  of  traditional  shopfronts.  Just

1891; the north gable, which is overlooking the street, features a pair of  narrow lancet windows.

Road. It was built in 1829 in a neo-Gothic style. The original church was small, but a chancel was
added in 1852 and the nave extended in the 1860s.

Ballydehob  is  the  access  gateway  to  the  Mizen  Peninsula  and  is  a  village  that  attracts  visitors  on

This  area  was  part  of  Pobbal  O’Keeffe,  that  part  of  North  Cork  occupied  by  the  Uí  Chaoimh
who were pushed west from their traditional homeland around Glanworth by the arrival of  the
Normans  in  the  12th  century.  Though  involved  in  the  various  rebellions  of  the  17th century, the
O’Keeffe’s  managed  to  hold  on  to  most  of  their  lands,  until  the Williamite  Confiscations.  In  1703
the British Government attempted to sell this land, some 8,500 acres, but without success, chiefly
because of  the poor quality of  the land and the remoteness of  the area (Ó Murchadha 1985, 44-
46).

Eventually, in 1827 it was decided to make the area more accessible by building a road over the
mountain  linking  Mallow  to  Castleisland  (O’Keeffe,  1980).  This  road  was  built  by  the  engineer
Richard  Griffith  who  also  undertook,  in  1832,  to  build  a  village  on  the  Cork  side  of  his  bridge
over  the  River  Blackwater,  which  here  marks  the  Cork-Kerry  border.  The  village  was  called
Kingwilliamstown, though the old name for the place was Tuairín Caoch - the blind little bleaching
green  (Bowman  2000,  300-331). The  village  was  small  and  in  1839  consisted  of  an  inn,  a  school
house,  four  two-storey  houses  and  seven  one-storey  houses.  The  area  around  the  village  was
eventually  sold  to  private  owners  in  1854.  The  village  name  was  changed  to  Ballydesmond  in
1933.

Today,  the  village  retains  its  19th  century  street  line,  with  two-storey  houses  lining  both  sides  of
the street. The Catholic church overlooks the village, c. 200 metres to the north. It was built in the
1880s  in  a  neo-Gothic  style,  with  sandstone  walls,  featuring  limestone  surrounds  to  doors  and
windows.

A village on the east shore of  Baltimore Bay. An important marine and tourist destination in West

The medieval settlement here was dominated by the O Driscoll castle of  Dún na Séad (fortress of
the  jewels),  which  overlooks  the  harbour.  The  O  Driscolls  were  noted  pirates,  and  this  was  their
chief  base for raiding along the south coast, as far east as Waterford Harbour (Kelleher 2020). The
clan  fell  on  hard  times  after  the  Irish  defeat  at  the  Battle  of  Kinsale  (1601 AD)  and  began  to  sell,
lease  and  mortgage  their  lands  to  English  adventurers  like  Thomas  Cooke.  Cooke  developed
Baltimore  as  an  English  settlement  and  a  map  of  1612  shows  a  bustling  fishing  village  centred
around  the  castle,  which  Cooke  now  occupied  as  his  headquarters.  In  1631  pirates  who  were
based in Algiers raided the village and notoriously carried off  many of  its inhabitants as slaves.
At  that  stage  the  village  contained  some  100  houses  with  a  population  of  around  500. After  this
raid the village probably went into decline and by 1750 was described as “a poor decayed fishing
town, with not one tolerable house in it” (Smith 1750, vol. 1, 268-272).

Dún na Séad castle

have been recently erected … and in 1833 a substantial pier was constructed.” Lewis does remark
that there was neither a fair nor a market in Baltimore, so the village was largely dependent on
the sea for its prosperity.

Placename Meaning:Bandon bridge Population 2016: 6,957

Today, Bandon is a vibrant commercial market town, on the Bandon River, c. 32 kilometres west of
Cork City. It was founded in the early 1600’s as part of  the Munster Plantation following the defeat
of  the Irish at the Battle of  Kinsale (1601).

The  town  began  as  two  distinct  settlements,  founded  by  William  Newce  and  John  Archdeacon,
on  either  side  of  the  Bandon  River  and  was  reserved  for  English  Protestants  settlers.  The  native
population were concentrated in a suburb, known as Irish Town, located to the east of  the town in
the area now occupied by Oliver Plunkett Street. In 1613 both settlements were united and were
incorporated as a single municipal and parliamentary borough.

In 1618, the fledgling planter settlements were bought by the powerful First Earl of  Cork, Richard
Boyle,  who  built  town  walls  to  protect  the  inhabitants. Apart  from  Derry,  Bandon  is  the  only  Irish
plantation  town  that  still  retains  parts  of  its  walls  and  it  is  proud  to  be  part  of  the  Irish  Walled
Towns Network. It hosts a successful Walled Town Festival every year.

Rare  examples  survive  of  some  17th  century  buildings  including  Christ  Church  (21)  and  No.  83
North  Main  Street  (22).  In  1753  the  Boyle  estates,  including  Bandon,  passed  through  marriage
to the Dukes of  Devonshire who funded the construction of  many fine public buildings, terraces,
markets and quays and who maintained a system of  wells and pumps.

Bandon,  like  many  Irish  towns,  was  substantially  rebuilt  in  the  late  18th  /  early  19th century
with  elegant,  well-proportioned  Georgian  streetscapes,  best  seen  on  Kilbrogan  Hill.  From  its
foundation, the town was known for the manufacture of  wool, linen and cotton.

A panoramic view of Bandon, with St. Peter’s Church of Ireland on the right

By  the  early  19th  century,  it  had  numerous  industrial  activities  including  five  breweries,  two
distilleries, a flour mill and nine tanneries. The town has a wide variety of  historic places of  worship
Anglican,  Methodist,  Presbyterian  and  Roman  Catholic  -  reflecting  its  interesting  historical  past.

Bantry is a lively market town at the head of  Bantry Bay, in West Cork.

The  earliest  known  settlement  in  the  area  is  the  Early  Christian  monastery  at  Kilnaruane
overlooking the town. The Normans invaded in the early 13th century and established a castle at
Dunnamark but soon retreated. It was the Gaelic O’Sullivan Lordship of  Beara that dominated the
area in later Medieval times.

The  first  small  settlement  in  the  current  location  was  established  in  1600  by  English  settlers
keen  to  exploit  the  rich  pilchard  fisheries  of  Bantry  Bay.  After  the  turbulent  17th century, the
town prospered and developed under the watchful eye of  the Landlord Richard White, who had
recently purchased the large estate. The town’s population grew rapidly and by 1725 there were
numerous fish processing plants, known as “fish palaces”, where fish oil was extracted. Merchant
ships  visited  regularly  to  transport  local  produce  including  cured  and  salted  fish.  The  town
expanded, arching over the river to create Bridge Street and New Street.

During  the  1800s,  the  pilchard  fisheries  declined  but  other  industries  such  as  tanning,  flour
milling,  textile  production,  iron  smelting  and  brewing  were  established.  Cereals,  butter,  pork,
and  beef  were  shipped  out  in  great  quantities  and  new  quays  and  piers  were  built.  However,
the  area  was  badly  hit  by  the  famine  years  of  the  mid-19th  century.  By  the  late  19th century, the
development  of  new  roads  into  West  Cork  and  the  arrival  of  the  railway  in  1881  revived  the
town’s commercial activity. Tourism also flourished and Bantry became a popular destination.

The  present  town  retains  much  of  its  18th  /  19th century character, with an elegant streetscape of
two and three storey houses, as well as many original civic buildings. The survival of  numerous
traditional shop fronts reflects the commercial vibrancy of  the town in the past. The town continues
to be a lively commercial centre with numerous music and cultural events and is well known for
its  market  with  local  crafts  and  artisan  foods.  Also  in  the  town,  just  off  Wolfe  Tone  Square,  is  a
wonderful museum, run by the Bantry Historical Society.

the pier (Lower) and the second, at the older parish centre to the south (Upper).

A village at the western end of  the Beara Peninsula, surrounded by the rugged hilly landscape of

The mining for copper ore began here in 1812 when John Puxley, whose ancestors were smugglers
from  West  Cork,  founded  the  Allihies  Mining  Company.  Through  skilful  management,  Puxley
