### Carvings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Carvings")]

The greater part of the stone carving of Wells Cathedral comprises foliate capitals in the stiff-leaf style. They are found ornamenting the piers of the nave, choir and transepts. Stiff-leaf foliage is highly abstract. Though possibly influenced by carvings of [acanthus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acanthus_(ornament) "Acanthus (ornament)") leaves or [vine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grape "Grape") leaves, it cannot be easily identified with any particular plant.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor196777%E2%80%9379-125) Here the carving of the foliage is varied and vigorous, the springing leaves and deep undercuts casting shadows that contrast with the surface of the piers.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor196777%E2%80%9379-125) In the transepts and towards the crossing in the nave the capitals have many small figurative carvings among the leaves. These include a man with toothache and a series of four scenes depicting the "[Wages of Sin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistle_to_the_Romans "Epistle to the Romans")" in a narrative of fruit stealers who creep into an orchard and are then beaten by the farmer. Another well-known carving is in the north transept aisle: a foliate [corbel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corbel "Corbel"), on which climbs a lizard, sometimes identified as a [salamander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salamander_(legendary_creature) "Salamander (legendary creature)"), a symbol of [eternal life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eternal_life_(Christianity) "Eternal life (Christianity)").[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwaan1984193-116)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor196777%E2%80%9379-125)

Carvings in the Decorated Gothic style may be found in the eastern end of the buildings, where there are many carved bosses. In the chapter house, the carvings of the 51 stalls include numerous small heads of great variety, many of them smiling or laughing. A well-known figure is the corbel of the dragon-slaying monk in the chapter house stair. The large continuous capital that encircles the central pillar of the chapter house is markedly different in style to the stiff-leaf of the Early English period. In contrast to the bold projections and undercutting of the earlier work, it has a rippling form and is clearly identifiable as grapevine.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor1967156%E2%80%93157-126)

The 15th-century cloisters have many small bosses ornamenting the vault. Two in the west cloister, near the gift shop and café, have been called [sheela na gigs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheela_na_gig "Sheela na gig"), i. e. female figures displaying their genitals and variously judged to depict the sin of [lust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lust "Lust") or stem from ancient fertility cults.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWarren200558-127)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTECave1948214-128)[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-129)

#### Misericords

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Misericords")]

Wells Cathedral has one of the finest sets of [misericords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misericord "Misericord") in Britain.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith19751%E2%80%932,_25-130)[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-EWebb-131) Its clergy has a long tradition of singing or reciting from the [Book of Psalms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Psalms "Book of Psalms") each day, along with the customary daily reading of the [Holy Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liturgy_of_the_Hours "Liturgy of the Hours"). In medieval times the clergy assembled in the church eight times daily for the [canonical hours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canonical_hours "Canonical hours"). As the greater part of the services was recited while standing, many monastic or collegiate churches fitted stalls whose seats tipped up to provide a ledge for the monk or cleric to lean against. These were "misericords" because their installation was an act of mercy.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith19751%E2%80%932,_25-130) Misericords typically have a carved figurative bracket beneath the ledge framed by two floral motifs known, in [heraldic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heraldry "Heraldry") manner, as "supporters".[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith19751%E2%80%93

**Wells Cathedral**, formally the _Cathedral Church of [St Andrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew\_the\_Apostle "Andrew the Apostle")_, is a [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England") cathedral in [Wells, Somerset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells,_Somerset "Wells, Somerset"), England. It is the seat of the [bishop of Bath and Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Bath_and_Wells "Bishop of Bath and Wells") and the [mother church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mother_church "Mother church") of the [diocese of Bath and Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocese_of_Bath_and_Wells "Diocese of Bath and Wells"). There are daily Church of England services in the building, and in 2023 it was reported to receive over 300,000 visitors per year.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-4) The cathedral is a [Grade I listed building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grade_I_listed_building "Grade I listed building").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-ehlisting-1) The cathedral precincts contain the [Bishop's Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Palace,_Wells "Bishop's Palace, Wells") and several buildings linked to its medieval chapter of [secular canons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canon_(priest) "Canon (priest)"), including the fifteenth-century [Vicars' Close](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicars'_Close,_Wells "Vicars' Close, Wells").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwaan1984188%E2%80%93196-5)

The earliest record of a church on the present site is a charter of 766.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-ehlisting-1) A bishopric was established in 909; however in 1090 the cathedral of the diocese was moved to [Bath Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bath_Abbey "Bath Abbey") and remained there until Wells became co-cathedral in 1218.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-ehlisting-1)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-:0-6) The remains of the tenth-century cathedral lie to the south of the present building, beneath the cloister. The present cathedral has a [cruciform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cruciform "Cruciform") plan with a [chapter house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapter_house "Chapter house") attached to the north and a [cloister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloister "Cloister") to the south, and is largely the result of two building campaigns which took place between c.1180 to c.1260 and c.1285 to c.1345. The western half of the cathedral, including the nave and western [transepts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transept "Transept"), belongs primarily to the first building phase and is constructed in the [Early English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_English_(architecture) "Early English (architecture)") style of [Gothic architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_architecture "Gothic architecture"). The east end, including the [lady chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_chapel "Lady chapel"), eastern transepts, chapter house, and central tower, belongs to the second phase and uses the [Decorated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decorated_(architecture) "Decorated (architecture)") Gothic style and retains much medieval [stained glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stained_glass "Stained glass").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-ehlisting-1)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-:0-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor1967274-7) Two towers were added to the west front between 1385 and 1410 in the [Perpendicular Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpendicular_Gothic "Perpendicular Gothic") style, and the cloisters were remodelled in the same style between 1420 and 1508. The cathedral was restored over the course of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-ehlisting-1)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-:0-6)

Wells has been called "unquestionably one of the most beautiful" and "most poetic" of English cathedrals.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-8)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor1967274-7) The architectural historian [John Harvey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Harvey_(historian) "John Harvey (historian)") sees it as Europe's first truly Gothic structure, breaking from the last constraints of the [Romanesque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanesque_architecture "Romanesque architecture") style.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarvey198719-9) The west front, which contains 300 sculpted figures,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor1967274-7) has been described by Harvey as the "supreme triumph of the combined plastic arts in England";[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarvey196163-10) however the architectural historian [Nikolaus Pevsner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolaus_Pevsner "Nikolaus Pevsner") described it as "spare", with "harsh uprights and horizontals [...] like steel scaffolding".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-:0-6)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Early years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early years")]

The earliest remains of a building on the site are of a late-[Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Britain "Roman Britain")[mausoleum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mausoleum "Mausoleum"), identified during excavations in 1980.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-pastscape-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAdkins1992118%E2%80%93119-12) An abbey church was built in Wells in 705 by [Aldhelm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aldhelm "Aldhelm"), first bishop of the newly established [Diocese of Sherborne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Sherborne "Bishop of Sherborne") during the reign of King [Ine of Wessex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ine_of_Wessex "Ine of Wessex").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-britania-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMalden194727-14) It was dedicated to [St Andrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_the_Apostle "Andrew the Apostle") and stood at the site of the cathedral's [cloisters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloister "Cloister"), where some excavated remains can be seen. There is a modern commemoration stone[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-15) to King Ine set in the floor of the Cathedral between the nave and the transept. The [font](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptismal_font "Baptismal font") in the cathedral's south [transept](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transept "Transept") is from this church and is the oldest part of the present building.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPepin2004141-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-17) In 766 [Cynewulf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynewulf_of_Wessex "Cynewulf of Wessex"), [King of Wessex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_monarchs_of_Wessex "List of monarchs of Wessex"), signed a charter endowing the church with eleven [hides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hide_(unit) "Hide (unit)") of land.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-Hides-19)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-LapidgeBlair2013-20)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-21) In 909 the seat of the diocese was moved from Sherborne to Wells.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-pastscape-11)

The first bishop of Wells was [Athelm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athelm "Athelm") (909), who crowned [King Æthelstan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%86thelstan "Æthelstan"). Athelm and his nephew [Dunstan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunstan "Dunstan") both became [Archbishops of Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archbishop_of_Canterbury "Archbishop of Canterbury").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-britania-13) During this period a choir of boys was established to sing the [liturgy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liturgy "Liturgy"). [Wells Cathedral School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral_School "Wells Cathedral School"), which was established to educate these choirboys, dates its foundation to this point.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-22) There is, however, some controversy over this. Following the [Norman Conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_conquest_of_England "Norman conquest of England"), [John de Villula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Tours "John of Tours") moved the seat of the bishop from Wells to Bath in 1090.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTETatton-BrownCrook200274%E2%80%9376-23) The church at Wells, no longer a cathedral, had a college of [secular clergy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secular_clergy "Secular clergy").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTETatton-BrownCrook200274%E2%80%9376-23)

### Seat of the bishop

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Seat of the bishop")]

The cathedral is thought to have been conceived and commenced in about 1175 by [Reginald Fitz Jocelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reginald_Fitz_Jocelin "Reginald Fitz Jocelin"), who died in 1191.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarvey198757-24)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPowicke1961251-25)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMatthews200513-26) Although it is clear from its size that from the outset, the church was planned to be the cathedral of the diocese,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTETatton-BrownCrook200274%E2%80%9376-23) the seat of the bishop moved between Wells and the abbeys of [Glastonbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glastonbury_Abbey "Glastonbury Abbey") and [Bath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bath_Abbey "Bath Abbey"), before settling at Wells. In 1197 Reginald's successor, [Savaric FitzGeldewin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savaric_FitzGeldewin "Savaric FitzGeldewin"), with the approval of [Pope Celestine III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Celestine_III "Pope Celestine III"), officially moved his seat to Glastonbury Abbey. The title of Bishop of Bath and Glastonbury was used until the Glastonbury claim was abandoned in 1219.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrooke1976184%E2%80%93185-27)

Savaric's successor, [Jocelin of Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jocelin_of_Wells "Jocelin of Wells"), again moved the bishop's seat to Bath Abbey, with the title Bishop of Bath. Jocelin was a brother of [Hugh (II) of Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_of_Wells "Hugh of Wells")[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-BHOBath-28) and was present at the signing of [Magna Carta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magna_Carta "Magna Carta"). Jocelin continued the building campaign begun by Reginald and was responsible for the [Bishop's Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Palace,_Wells "Bishop's Palace, Wells"), the [choristers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choir "Choir")' school, a [grammar school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammar_school "Grammar school"), a hospital for travellers and a chapel. He also had a manor house built at [Wookey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wookey "Wookey"), near Wells.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-DNB-29) Jocelin saw the church dedicated in 1239 but, despite much lobbying of the Pope by Jocelin's representatives in Rome, he did not live to see cathedral status granted. The delay may have been a result of inaction by [Pandulf Verraccio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandulf_Verraccio "Pandulf Verraccio"), a Roman ecclesiastical politician, papal legate to England and [Bishop of Norwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Norwich "Bishop of Norwich"), who was asked by the Pope to investigate the situation but did not respond.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColchester198715-30) Jocelin died at Wells on 19 November 1242 and was buried in the choir of the cathedral;[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-BHOBath-28)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-DNB-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFryde1986228-31) the [memorial brass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monumental_brass "Monumental brass") on his tomb is one of the earliest brasses in England.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-DNB-29) Following his death the monks of Bath unsuccessfully attempted to regain authority over Wells.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobinson1916161-32)

In 1245 the ongoing dispute over the title of the bishop was resolved by a ruling of [Pope Innocent IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Innocent_IV "Pope Innocent IV"), who established the title as the "Bishop of Bath and Wells", which it has remained until this day, with Wells as the principal seat of the bishop.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDunning200141-33) Since the 11th century the church has had a [chapter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathedral_chapter "Cathedral chapter") of secular clergy, like the cathedrals of [Chichester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chichester_Cathedral "Chichester Cathedral"), [Hereford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hereford_Cathedral "Hereford Cathedral"), [Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_Cathedral "Lincoln Cathedral") and [York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York_Minster "York Minster"). The chapter was endowed with 22 [prebends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prebendary "Prebendary") (lands from which finance was drawn) and a provost to manage them. On acquiring cathedral status, in common with other such cathedrals, it had four chief clergy, the [dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dean_(Christianity) "Dean (Christianity)"), [precentor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precentor "Precentor"), [chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_(ecclesiastical) "Chancellor (ecclesiastical)") and [sacristan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacristan "Sacristan"), who were responsible for the spiritual and material care of the cathedral.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-CofEmedia-34)

### Building the cathedral

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Building the cathedral")]

The building programme, begun by Reginald Fitz Jocelin, bishop in the 12th century, continued under Jocelin of Wells, who was a canon from 1200, then bishop from 1206. Adam Locke was master mason from about 1192 until 1230.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarvey1987163-35) It was designed in the new style with pointed arches, later known as [Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_architecture "Gothic architecture"), which was introduced at about the same time at [Canterbury Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_Cathedral "Canterbury Cathedral").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarvey198757%E2%80%9358-36) Work was halted between 1209 and 1213 when [King John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John,_King_of_England "John, King of England") was [excommunicated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excommunication "Excommunication") and Jocelin was in exile,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReid196340%E2%80%9341-37) but the main parts of the church were complete by the time of the dedication by Jocelin in 1239.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTETatton-BrownCrook200274%E2%80%9376-23)

By the time the cathedral, including the [chapter house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapter_house "Chapter house"), was finished in 1306,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-sacred-38) it was already too small for the developing liturgy, and unable to accommodate increasingly grand processions of clergy. [John Droxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Droxford "John Droxford") initiated another phase of building under master mason Thomas of Whitney,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-sacred-38) during which the central tower was heightened and an eight-sided [Lady chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_chapel "Lady chapel") was added at the east end by 1326.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-isleofavalon-39)[Ralph of Shrewsbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_of_Shrewsbury "Ralph of Shrewsbury") followed, continuing the eastward extension of the choir and [retrochoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retrochoir "Retrochoir") beyond. He oversaw the building of [Vicars' Close](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicars'_Close,_Wells "Vicars' Close, Wells") and the Vicars' Hall, to give the men who were employed to sing in the choir a secure place to live and dine, away from the town and its temptations.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-localhist-40) He had an uneasy relationship with the citizens of Wells, partly because of his imposition of taxes,[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-localhist-40) and he surrounded his palace with [crenellated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battlement "Battlement") walls, a moat and a drawbridge.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-41)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-42)

[John Harewell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Harewell "John Harewell") raised money for the completion of the west front by [William Wynford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Wynford "William Wynford"), who was appointed as master mason in 1365. One of the foremost master masons of his time, Wynford worked for the king at [Windsor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windsor,_Berkshire "Windsor, Berkshire"), [Winchester Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winchester_Cathedral "Winchester Cathedral") and [New College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_College,_Oxford "New College, Oxford").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarvey1987352-43) At Wells, he designed the western towers, the north-west of which was not built until the following century.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWade1926257-44) In the 14th century, the central [piers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pier_(architecture) "Pier (architecture)") of the [crossing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossing_(architecture) "Crossing (architecture)") were found to be sinking under the weight of the crossing tower which had been damaged by an earthquake in the previous century.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-cathbrit-45)[Strainer arches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strainer_arch "Strainer arch"), sometimes described as scissor arches, were inserted by master mason [William Joy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Joy "William Joy") to brace and stabilise the piers as a unit.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-cathbrit-45)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-46)

### Tudors and Civil War

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Tudors and Civil War")]

By the reign of [Henry VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VII_of_England "Henry VII of England") the cathedral was complete, appearing much as it does today (though the fittings have changed). From 1508 to 1546, the eminent Italian [humanist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_humanism "Renaissance humanism") scholar [Polydore Vergil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polydore_Vergil "Polydore Vergil") was active as the chapter's representative in London. He donated a set of hangings for the [choir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choir_(architecture) "Choir (architecture)") of the cathedral.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHay19528%E2%80%9320-47)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-48) While Wells survived the [Dissolution of the Monasteries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Monasteries "Dissolution of the Monasteries") better than the cathedrals of monastic foundation, the abolition of chantries in 1547 resulted in a reduction in its income. [Medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages") brasses were sold, and a [pulpit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulpit "Pulpit") was placed in the [nave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nave "Nave") for the first time.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-49) Between 1551 and 1568, in two periods as dean, [William Turner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Turner_(naturalist) "William Turner (naturalist)") established a [herb garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_garden "Herb garden"), which was recreated between 2003 and 2010.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-50)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-51)

[Elizabeth I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_I_of_England "Elizabeth I of England") gave the chapter and the Vicars Choral a new charter in 1591, creating a new governing body, consisting of a dean and eight residentiary canons with control over the church estates and authority over its affairs, but no longer entitled to elect the dean (that entitlement thenceforward belonged ultimately to [the Crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crown "The Crown")).[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-52) The stability brought by the new charter ended with the onset of the [Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Civil_War "English Civil War") and the execution of [Charles I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England"). Local fighting damaged the cathedral's stonework, furniture and windows. The dean, [Walter Raleigh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Raleigh_(priest) "Walter Raleigh (priest)"), a nephew of the explorer [Walter Raleigh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Raleigh "Walter Raleigh"), was placed under house arrest after the fall of [Bridgwater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridgwater "Bridgwater") to the [Parliamentarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundhead "Roundhead") in 1645, first in the rectory at [Chedzoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chedzoy "Chedzoy") and then in the deanery at Wells.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-53) His jailor, the shoe maker and city constable, David Barrett, caught him writing a letter to his wife. When he refused to surrender it, Barrett ran him through with a sword and he died six weeks later, on 10 October 1646.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-bbc-parod-54) He was buried in an unmarked grave in the choir before the dean's stall.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-55) During the [Commonwealth of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_England "Commonwealth of England") under [Oliver Cromwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell") no dean was appointed and the cathedral fell into disrepair. The bishop went into retirement and some of the clerics were reduced to performing menial tasks.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-56)

### 1660–1800

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 1660–1800")]

In 1661, after [Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England "Charles II of England") was [restored to the throne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Restoration "Stuart Restoration"), [Robert Creighton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Creighton_(1593%E2%80%931672) "Robert Creighton (1593–1672)"), the king's chaplain in exile, was appointed dean and was bishop for two years before his death in 1672.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTELehmberg199655-57) His brass [lectern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lectern "Lectern"), given in thanksgiving, can be seen in the cathedral. He donated the nave's great west window at a cost of £140. Following Creighton's appointment as bishop, the post of dean went to [Ralph Bathurst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Bathurst "Ralph Bathurst"), who had been chaplain to the king, president of [Trinity College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_College,_Oxford "Trinity College, Oxford") and fellow of the [Royal Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Society "Royal Society").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHopkins2005161-58) During Bathurst's long tenure the cathedral was restored, but in the [Monmouth Rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monmouth_Rebellion "Monmouth Rebellion") of 1685, Puritan soldiers damaged the west front, tore lead from the roof to make bullets, broke the windows, smashed the organ and furnishings, and for a time stabled their horses in the nave.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-59)

Restoration began again under [Thomas Ken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Ken "Thomas Ken") who was appointed by the Crown in 1685 and served until 1691. He was one of seven bishops imprisoned for refusing to sign [King James II's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_II_of_England "James II of England") "[Declaration of Indulgence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_of_Indulgence_(1687) "Declaration of Indulgence (1687)")", which would have enabled Catholics to resume positions of political power, but popular support led to their acquittal. Ken refused to take the oath of allegiance to [William III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_III_of_England "William III of England") and [Mary II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_II_of_England "Mary II of England") because James II had not abdicated and with others, known as the [Nonjurors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonjuring_schism "Nonjuring schism"), was put out of office.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-60) His successor, [Richard Kidder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Kidder "Richard Kidder"), was killed in the [Great Storm of 1703](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Storm_of_1703 "Great Storm of 1703") when two chimney stacks on the palace fell on him and his wife, while they were asleep in bed.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-61)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-62)

The 13th-century west front was vandalised during the Monmouth Rebellion, destroying many of the carved figures and leaving others, like those of the _Coronation of the Virgin_, headless.

The choir stalls have 19th-century stone canopies and modern embroideries commemorating bishops. The 19th century saw the restoration of the building and its fittings.

### Victorian era to present

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Victorian era to present")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/A._R._Quinton%2C_Wells_Cathedral_from_Tor_Hill.jpg/250px-A._R._Quinton%2C_Wells_Cathedral_from_Tor_Hill.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:A._R._Quinton,_Wells_Cathedral_from_Tor_Hill.jpg)

[A. R. Quinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._R._Quinton "A. R. Quinton"), Wells Cathedral from Tor Hill, c. 1920

By the middle of the 19th century, a major [restoration programme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_restoration "Victorian restoration") was needed. Under [Dean Goodenough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_Goodenough "Edmund Goodenough"), the monuments were moved to the cloisters and the remaining medieval paint and [whitewash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitewash "Whitewash") removed in an operation known as "the great scrape".[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-63)[Anthony Salvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Salvin "Anthony Salvin") took charge of the extensive restoration of the choir. Wooden galleries installed in the 16th century were removed and the stalls were given stone canopies and placed further back within the line of the arcade. The medieval stone [pulpitum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulpitum "Pulpitum") screen was extended in the centre to support a new organ.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColchester1987126%E2%80%93127-64)

In 1933 the Friends of Wells Cathedral were formed to support the cathedral's chapter in the maintenance of the fabric, life and work of the cathedral.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-65) The late 20th century saw an extensive restoration programme, particularly of the west front.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHatton1999218%E2%80%93230-66)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-westfrontrestore-67) The stained glass is currently under restoration, with a programme underway to conserve the large 14th-century [Jesse Tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tree_of_Jesse "Tree of Jesse") window at the eastern terminal of the choir.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-68)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-vidimus-69)

In January 2014, as part of the [Bath film festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bath_film_festival "Bath film festival"), the cathedral hosted a special screening of [Martin Scorsese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Scorsese "Martin Scorsese")'s _[The Last Temptation of Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Last\_Temptation\_of\_Christ\_(film) "The Last Temptation of Christ (film)")_. This provoked some controversy, but the church defended its decision to allow the screening.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-70)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-71) In 2021, a contemporary sculpture by [Antony Gormley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antony_Gormley "Antony Gormley") was unveiled on a temporary plinth outside the cathedral.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-72)

In April 2025, another major restoration of the Cathedral's western front began.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-73)

## Ministry

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Ministry")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Wells_Cathedral_in_the_reflecting_pool_in_the_grounds_of_the_Bishops_Palace.jpg/250px-Wells_Cathedral_in_the_reflecting_pool_in_the_grounds_of_the_Bishops_Palace.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wells_Cathedral_in_the_reflecting_pool_in_the_grounds_of_the_Bishops_Palace.jpg)

From the [reflecting pool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reflecting_pool "Reflecting pool") in the grounds of the [Bishop's Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_Palace,_Wells "Bishop's Palace, Wells")

Since the 13th century, Wells Cathedral has been the seat of the [Bishop of Bath and Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Bath_and_Wells "Bishop of Bath and Wells"). Its governing body, the [chapter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapter_(religion) "Chapter (religion)"), is made up of five clerical canons (the dean, the precentor, the canon chancellor, the canon treasurer, and the [Archdeacon of Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archdeacon_of_Wells "Archdeacon of Wells")) and four lay members: the administrator, the Keeper of the Fabric, the Overseer of the Estate, and the chairman of the cathedral shop and catering boards.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-Chapter-74) The current bishop of Bath and Wells is [Michael Beesley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Beasley_(bishop) "Michael Beasley (bishop)"), who was installed in a service in the cathedral on 19 November 2022.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-75) The current [dean of Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dean_of_Wells "Dean of Wells") is [Toby Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toby_Wright_(priest) "Toby Wright (priest)"), who was installed on 16 June 2024.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-76)

Staff include the organist and master of choristers, head Verger archivist, librarian and the staff of the shop, café and restaurant.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-77) The chapter is advised by specialists such as architects, archaeologists and financial analysts.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-Chapter-74)

More than a thousand services are held every year. There are daily services of [Matins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matins "Matins"), Holy Communion and Choral Evensong,[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-78) as well as major celebrations of Christian festivals such as Christmas, Easter, [Pentecost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentecost "Pentecost") and [saints' days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint's_Day "Saint's Day").[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-79) The cathedral is also used for the baptisms, weddings and funerals of those with close connections to it.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-80) In July 2009 the cathedral undertook the funeral of [Harry Patch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Patch "Harry Patch"), the last [British Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Army "British Army") veteran of [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), who died at the age of 111.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-81)

Three Sunday services are led by the resident choir in school terms and choral services are sung on weekdays. The cathedral hosts visiting choirs and does outreach work with local schools as part of its Chorister Outreach Project.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-82) It is also a venue for musical events such as an annual concert by the [Somerset Chamber Choir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerset_Chamber_Choir "Somerset Chamber Choir").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-83)

Each year about 150,000 people attend services and another 300,000 visit as tourists.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-84)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-85) General admission tickets can be purchased via the Welcome Desk. There is no charge for people who wish to come into the Cathedral to pray, attend a service, or light a candle.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-86)

## Architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Architecture")]

### Dates, styles and architects

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Dates, styles and architects")]

[![Image 16](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9d/WellsCathPlan_numbered.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:WellsCathPlan_numbered.JPG)

Plan of Wells Cathedral:[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-87)

1.   West front
2.   Nave
3.   Central tower
4.   Choir
5.   Retrochoir
6.   Lady Chapel
7.   Aisle
8.   Transept
9.   East transept
10.   North porch
11.   Chapter house
12.   Cloister

Construction of the cathedral began in about 1175, to the design of an unknown master-mason. Wells is the first cathedral in England to be built, from its foundation, in Gothic style. According to art historian [John Harvey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Harvey_(historian) "John Harvey (historian)"), it is the first truly Gothic cathedral in the world, its architects having entirely dispensed with all features that bound the contemporary east end of Canterbury Cathedral and the earlier buildings of France, such as the east end of the [Abbey of Saint Denis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilica_of_St_Denis "Basilica of St Denis"), to the Romanesque.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarvey198719-9) Unlike these churches, Wells has clustered piers rather than columns and has a gallery of identical pointed arches rather than the typically Romanesque form of paired openings. The style, with its simple [lancet arches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancet_arch "Lancet arch") without tracery and convoluted mouldings, is known as [Early English Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_English_Gothic "Early English Gothic").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFletcher1961189%E2%80%93190-88)

From about 1192 to 1230, Adam Lock, the earliest master-mason at Wells for whom a name is known, continued the transept and nave in the same manner as his predecessor. Lock was also the builder of the north porch, to his own design.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarvey1987163-35)

The Early English west front was commenced around 1230 by Thomas Norreys, with building and sculpture continuing for thirty years.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarvey1987163-35) Its south-west tower was begun 100 years later and constructed between 1365 and 1395, and the north-west tower between 1425 and 1435,[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-89) both in the [Perpendicular Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpendicular_Gothic "Perpendicular Gothic") style to the design of William Wynford,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarvey1987163-35) who also filled many of the cathedral's early English [lancet windows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancet_window "Lancet window") with delicate [tracery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracery "Tracery").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWade1926257-44)

The [undercroft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undercroft "Undercroft") and chapter house were built by unknown architects between 1275 and 1310, the undercroft in the Early English and the chapter house in the Geometric style of [Decorated Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decorated_Gothic "Decorated Gothic") architecture. In about 1310 work commenced on the Lady Chapel, to the design of [Thomas Witney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Witney "Thomas Witney"), who also built the central tower from 1315 to 1322 in the Decorated Gothic style.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarvey1987163-35) The tower was later braced internally with arches by William Joy.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarvey1987163-35) Concurrent with this work, in 1329–45 Joy made alterations and extensions to the choir, joining it to the Lady Chapel with the retrochoir, the latter in the [Flowing Decorated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flowing_Decorated "Flowing Decorated") style.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarvey1987163-35)

Later changes include the Perpendicular vault of the tower and construction of Sugar's Chapel, 1475–1490 by [William Smyth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Smyth_(architect) "William Smyth (architect)"). Also, Gothic Revival renovations were made to the choir and pulpitum by [Benjamin Ferrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Ferrey "Benjamin Ferrey") and Anthony Salvin, 1842–1857. Fletcher claims Ferry practically rebuilt the central tower in facsimile adding only several pinnacles [[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarvey1987163-35)

### Plan

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Plan")]

Wells has a total length of 415 feet (126 m). Like Canterbury, Lincoln and [Salisbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salisbury_Cathedral "Salisbury Cathedral") cathedrals, it has the distinctly English arrangement of two transepts, with the body of the church divided into distinct parts: nave, choir, and retrochoir, beyond which extends the Lady Chapel.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwaan1984173%E2%80%93174-90) The façade is wide, with its towers extending beyond the transepts on either side.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwaan1984188%E2%80%93196-5) There is a large projecting porch on the north side of the nave forming an entry into the cathedral.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPevsner1958278%E2%80%93310-91) To the north-east is the large octagonal chapter house, entered from the north choir aisle by a passage and staircase. To the south of the nave is a large cloister, unusual in that the northern range, that adjacent the cathedral, was never built.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor1967136-92)

### Elevation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Elevation")]

In section, the cathedral has the usual arrangement of a large church: a central nave with an aisle on each side, separated by two arcades. The elevation is in three stages, [arcade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcade_(architecture) "Arcade (architecture)"), [triforium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triforium "Triforium") gallery and [clerestory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clerestory "Clerestory").[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPevsner1958278%E2%80%93310-91) The nave is 67 feet (20 m) in height, very low compared to the Gothic cathedrals of France.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor196774%E2%80%9379-93) It has a markedly horizontal emphasis, caused by the triforium having a unique form, a series of identical narrow openings, lacking the usual definition of the bays. The triforium is separated from the arcade by a single horizontal [string course](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_course "String course") that runs unbroken the length of the nave. There are no vertical lines linking the three stages, as the shafts supporting the vault rise above the triforium.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPevsner1958278%E2%80%93310-91)

The cathedral from the south east. To the right of the central tower is the choir with the Lady Chapel projecting beyond it, and the chapter house, extreme right.

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/Wells_Cathedral_Central_Tower_Oct_2021.jpg/120px-Wells_Cathedral_Central_Tower_Oct_2021.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wells_Cathedral_Central_Tower_Oct_2021.jpg)

The central tower, nave and south transept seen from the cloister [garth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garth_(architecture) "Garth (architecture)"). The nave rises above the pitched roof of the aisle. The buttresses are of low profile.

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Wells_cathedral_nave_clerestory.JPG/250px-Wells_cathedral_nave_clerestory.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wells_cathedral_nave_clerestory.JPG)

The internal elevation of the nave is in three levels: arcade, triforium gallery and clerestory. The triforium has a unique form with the arches not grouped into bays.

### Exterior

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Exterior")]

The exterior of Wells Cathedral presents a relatively tidy and harmonious appearance since the greater part of the building was executed in a single style, [Early English Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_English_Gothic "Early English Gothic"). This is uncommon among English cathedrals where the exterior usually exhibits a plethora of styles.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-reeve-94) At Wells, later changes in the Perpendicular style were universally applied, such as filling the Early English lancet windows with simple tracery, the construction of a [parapet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parapet "Parapet") that encircles the roof, and the addition of [pinnacles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinnacle "Pinnacle") framing each [gable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gable "Gable"), similar to those around the chapter house and on the west front.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPevsner1958278%E2%80%93310-91) At the eastern end there is a proliferation of tracery with repeated motifs in the Reticulated style, a stage between Geometric and Flowing Decorated tracery.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor1967156%E2%80%93158-95)

#### West front

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: West front")]

The west front is 100 feet (30 m) high and 147 feet (45 m) wide,[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColchester1987183-96) and built of [Inferior Oolite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inferior_Oolite "Inferior Oolite") of the [Middle Jurassic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Jurassic "Middle Jurassic") period, which came from the [Doulting Stone Quarry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doulting_Stone_Quarry "Doulting Stone Quarry"), about 8 miles (13 km) to the east.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-97) According to the [architectural historian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architectural_historian "Architectural historian")[Alec Clifton-Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alec_Clifton-Taylor "Alec Clifton-Taylor"), it is "one of the great sights of England".[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor196778-98)

West fronts in general take three distinct forms: those that follow the elevation of the nave and aisles, those that have paired towers at the end of each aisle, framing the nave, and those that screen the form of the building. The west front at Wells has the paired-tower form, unusual in that the towers do not indicate the location of the aisles, but extend well beyond them, screening the dimensions and profile of the building.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwaan1984188%E2%80%93196-5)

The west front rises in three distinct stages, each clearly defined by a horizontal course. This horizontal emphasis is counteracted by six strongly projecting buttresses defining the cross-sectional divisions of nave, aisles and towers, and are highly decorated, each having canopied niches containing the largest statues on the façade.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor196778-98)

At the lowest level of the façade is a plain base, contrasting with and stabilising the ornate arcades that rise above it.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor196778-98) The base is penetrated by three doors, which are in stark contrast to the often imposing portals of French Gothic cathedrals. The outer two are of domestic proportion and the central door is ornamented only by a central post, [quatrefoil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quatrefoil "Quatrefoil") and the fine mouldings of the arch.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwaan1984188%E2%80%93196-5)

Above the basement rise two storeys, ornamented with quatrefoils and niches originally holding about four hundred statues, with three hundred surviving until the mid-20th century.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwaan1984188%E2%80%93196-5) Since then, some have been restored or replaced, including the ruined figure of Christ in the gable.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-Caroe-99)

The third stages of the flanking towers were both built in the Perpendicular style of the late 14th century, to the design of William Wynford; that on the north-west was not begun until about 1425.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarvey1987163-35) The design maintains the general proportions, and continues the strong projection of the buttresses.

The finished product has been criticised for its lack of pinnacles, and it is probable that the towers were intended to carry spires which were never built.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPevsner1958278%E2%80%93310-91) Despite its lack of spires or pinnacles, the architectural historian [Banister Fletcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banister_Fletcher_(junior) "Banister Fletcher (junior)") describes it as "the highest development in English Gothic of this type of façade."[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFletcher1961421-100)

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/Wells_cathedral_28_crop.JPG/250px-Wells_cathedral_28_crop.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wells_cathedral_28_crop.JPG)

The 13th-century west front by Thomas Norreys. As a synthesis of form, architectural decoration and figurative sculpture it is considered to be unsurpassed in Britain.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor196778-98)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarvey196163-10)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFletcher1961421-100)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwaan1984188%E2%80%93196-5)

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/Wells_cathedral_26.JPG/250px-Wells_cathedral_26.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wells_cathedral_26.JPG)

_Christ the Judge_, (late 20th-century) occupies the gable. Beneath are twelve apostles and nine archangels.

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Wells_cathedral_16.JPG/250px-Wells_cathedral_16.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wells_cathedral_16.JPG)

The strongly projecting buttresses have niches for statues.

##### Iconography of the west front

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Iconography of the west front")]

The sculptures on the west front at Wells include standing figures, seated figures, half-length angels and narratives in high relief. Many of the figures are life-sized or larger. Together they constitute the finest display of medieval carving in England.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwaan1984188%E2%80%93196-5) The figures and many of the architectural details were painted in bright colours, and the colouring scheme has been deduced from flakes of paint still adhering to some surfaces.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwaan1984188%E2%80%93196-5) The sculptures occupy nine architectural zones stretching horizontally across the entire west front and around the sides and the eastern [returns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return_(architecture) "Return (architecture)") of the towers which extend beyond the aisles. The strongly projecting buttresses have tiers of niches which contain many of the largest figures. Other large figures, including that of Christ, occupy the gable. A single figure stands in one of two later niches high on the northern tower.

In 1851 the archaeologist [Charles Robert Cockerell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Robert_Cockerell "Charles Robert Cockerell") published his analysis of the iconography, numbering the nine sculptural divisions from the lowest to the highest. He defined the theme as "a calendar for unlearned men" illustrating the doctrines and history of the Christian faith, its introduction to Britain and its protection by princes and bishops.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTECockerell185126-101) He likens the arrangement and iconography to the [Te Deum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Te_Deum "Te Deum").[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTECockerell185134-102)

According to Cockerell, the side of the façade that is to the south of the central door is the more sacred and the scheme is divided accordingly.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTECockerell185127-103) The lowest range of niches each contained a standing figure, of which all but four figures on the west front, two on each side, have been destroyed. More have survived on the northern and eastern sides of the north tower. Cockerell speculates that those to the south of the portal represented prophets and patriarchs of the [Old Testament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Testament "Old Testament") while those to the north represented early missionaries to Britain, of which [Augustine of Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_of_Canterbury "Augustine of Canterbury"), [St Birinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Birinus "St Birinus"), and [Benedict Biscop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benedict_Biscop "Benedict Biscop") are identifiable by their [attributes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_symbolism "Saint symbolism").[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTECockerell185127%E2%80%9328-104) In the second zone, above each pair of standing figures, is a quatrefoil containing a half-length angel in relief, some of which have survived.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTECockerell185152-105) Between the gables of the niches are quatrefoils that contain a series of narratives from the Bible, with the Old Testament stories to the south, above the prophets and patriarchs, and those from the New Testament to the north.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTECockerell185153-106) A horizontal course runs around the west front dividing the architectural storeys at this point.

Above the course, zones four and five, as identified by Cockerell, contain figures which represent the Christian Church in Britain, with the spiritual lords such as bishops, abbots, abbesses and saintly founders of monasteries on the south, while kings, queens and princes occupy the north.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTECockerell185130-107) Many of the figures survive and many have been identified in the light of their various attributes. There is a hierarchy of size, with the more significant figures larger and enthroned in their niches rather than standing.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTECockerell185175-108) Immediately beneath the upper course are a series of small niches containing dynamic sculptures of the dead coming forth from their tombs on the [Day of Judgement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_of_Judgement "Day of Judgement"). Although naked, some of the dead are defined as royalty by their crowns and others as bishops by their [mitres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitre "Mitre"). Some emerge from their graves with joy and hope, and others with despair.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTECockerell185131-109)

The niches in the lowest zone of the gable contain nine angels, of which Cockerell identifies Michael, Gabriel, Raphael and Uriel.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTECockerell185132-110) In the next zone are the taller figures of the twelve apostles, some, such as John, Andrew and Bartholomew, clearly identifiable by the attributes that they carry.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTECockerell185133-111) The uppermost niches of the gable contained the figure of Christ the Judge at the centre, with the Virgin Mary on his right and John the Baptist on his left. The figures all suffered from [iconoclasm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iconoclasm "Iconoclasm").[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTECockerell185133-111) A new statue of Jesus was carved for the central niche, but the two side niches now contain [cherubim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherub "Cherub"). Christ and the Virgin Mary are also represented by now headless figures in a [Coronation of the Virgin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronation_of_the_Virgin "Coronation of the Virgin") in a niche above the central portal. A damaged figure of the Virgin and Christ Child occupies a quatrefoil in the [spandrel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spandrel "Spandrel") of the door.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTECockerell185129%E2%80%9330-112)

#### Crossing tower

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Crossing tower")]

The central tower appears to date from the early 13th century. It was substantially reconstructed in the early 14th century during the remodelling of the east end, necessitating the internal bracing of the piers a decade or so later. In the 14th century the tower was given a timber and lead spire which burnt down in 1439. The exterior was then reworked in the Perpendicular style and given the present parapet and pinnacles.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTETatton-BrownCrook200274%E2%80%9376-23) Alec Clifton-Taylor describes it as "outstanding even in Somerset, a county famed for the splendour of its church towers".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor1967274-7)

#### North porch

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: North porch")]

The north porch is described by art historian [Nikolaus Pevsner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolaus_Pevsner "Nikolaus Pevsner") as "sumptuously decorated", and intended as the main entrance.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPevsner1958278%E2%80%93310-91) Externally it is simple and rectangular with plain side walls. The entrance is a steeply arched portal framed by rich mouldings of eight shafts with stiff-leaf capitals each encircled by an [annular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annulet_(architecture) "Annulet (architecture)") moulding at middle height. Those on the left are figurative, containing images representing the martyrdom of St [Edmund the Martyr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_the_Martyr "Edmund the Martyr").[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPevsner1958278%E2%80%93310-91) The walls are lined with deep niches framed by narrow shafts with capitals and annulets like those of the portal. The path to the north porch is lined by four sculptures in Purbeck stone, each by [Mary Spencer Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Spencer_Watson "Mary Spencer Watson"), representing the symbols of the [Evangelists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Evangelists "Four Evangelists").[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-BMorley-113)

#### Cloisters

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Cloisters")]

The cloisters were built in the late 13th century and largely rebuilt from 1430 to 1508[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTETatton-BrownCrook200274%E2%80%9376-23)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarvey1987163-35) and have wide openings divided by [mullions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mullion "Mullion") and [transoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transom_(architectural) "Transom (architectural)"), and tracery in the Perpendicular Gothic style. The vault has [lierne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lierne_(vault) "Lierne (vault)") ribs that form octagons at the centre of each compartment, the joints of each rib having decorative [bosses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boss_(architecture) "Boss (architecture)").[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor1967226-114) The eastern range is of two storeys, of which the upper is the library built in the 15th century.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTETatton-BrownCrook200274%E2%80%9376-23)

Because Wells Cathedral was secular rather than monastic, cloisters were not a practical necessity. They were omitted from several other secular cathedrals but were built here and at Chichester. Explanations for their construction at these two secular cathedrals range from the processional to the aesthetic.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor1967136-92) As at Chichester, there is no northern range to the cloisters. In monastic cloisters it was the north range, benefiting most from winter sunlight, that was often used as a [scriptorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scriptorium "Scriptorium").[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrossley196267%E2%80%9368-115)

#### Restoration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Restoration")]

In 1969, when a large chunk of stone fell from a statue near the main door, it became apparent that there was an urgent need for restoration of the west front.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-westfrontrestore-67) Detailed studies of the stonework and of conservation practices were undertaken under the cathedral architect, [Alban D. R. Caroe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alban_Caroe "Alban Caroe") and a restoration committee formed.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-Caroe-99) The methods selected were those devised by Eve and Robert Baker. W. A. (Bert) Wheeler, clerk of works to the cathedral 1935–1978, had previously experimented with washing and surface treatment of architectural carvings on the building and his techniques were among those tried on the statues.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-Caroe-99)

The conservation was carried out between 1974 and 1986, wherever possible using non-invasive procedures such as washing with water and a solution of [lime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lime_(material) "Lime (material)"), filling gaps and damaged surfaces with soft mortar to prevent the ingress of water and stabilising statues that were fracturing through corrosion of metal dowels. The surfaces were finished by painting with a thin coat of mortar and [silane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silane "Silane") to resist further erosion and attack by pollutants.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-westfrontrestore-67)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-Caroe-99) The restoration of the façade revealed much paint adhering to the statues and their niches, indicating that it had once been brightly coloured.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-westfrontrestore-67)

### Interior

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Interior")]

#### Choir, transept and nave

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Choir, transept and nave")]

The particular character of this Early English interior is dependent on the proportions of the simple lancet arches. It is also dependent on the refinement of the architectural details, in particular the mouldings.

The arcade, which takes the same form in the nave, choir and transepts, is distinguished by the richness of both mouldings and carvings. Each pier of the arcade has a surface enrichment of 24 slender shafts in eight groups of three, rising beyond the [capitals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_(architecture) "Capital (architecture)") to form the deeply undulating mouldings of the arches.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor196774%E2%80%9379-93) The capitals themselves are remarkable for the vitality of the stylised foliage, in a style known as "[stiff-leaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stiff-leaf "Stiff-leaf")". The liveliness contrasts with the formality of the moulded shafts and the smooth unbroken areas of [ashlar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashlar "Ashlar") masonry in the spandrels. Each capital is different, and some contain small figures illustrating narratives.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor196774%E2%80%9379-93)

The vault of the nave rises steeply in a simple quadripartite form, in harmony with the nave arcade.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPevsner1958278%E2%80%93310-91) The eastern end of the choir was extended and the whole upper part elaborated in the second quarter of the 14th century by William Joy.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarvey1987163-35) The vault has a multiplicity of ribs in a net-like form, which is very different from that of the nave, and is perhaps a recreation in stone of a local type of compartmented wooden roof of which examples remain from the 15th century, including those at [St Cuthbert's Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_St_Cuthbert,_Wells "Church of St Cuthbert, Wells"), Wells.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwaan1984193-116) The vaults of the aisles of the choir also have a unique pattern.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPevsner1958278%E2%80%93310-91)

Until the early 14th century, the interior of the cathedral was in a unified style, but it was to undergo two significant changes, to the tower and to the eastern end. Between 1315 and 1322 the central tower was heightened and topped by a spire, which caused the piers that supported it to show signs of stress. In 1338 the mason William Joy employed an unorthodox solution by inserting low arches topped by inverted arches of similar dimensions, forming scissors-like structures.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTESAHC082008199%E2%80%93205-117) These arches brace the piers of the crossing on three sides, while the easternmost side is braced by a choir screen.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-118) The bracing arches are known as "St Andrew's Cross arches", in a reference to the patron saint of the cathedral. They have been described by Wim Swaan – rightly or wrongly – as "brutally massive" and intrusive in an otherwise restrained interior.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwaan1984188%E2%80%93196-5)

#### Lady Chapel and retrochoir

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Lady Chapel and retrochoir")]

Wells Cathedral has a square east end to the choir, as is usual, and like several other cathedrals including Salisbury and [Lichfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lichfield_Cathedral "Lichfield Cathedral"), has a lower Lady Chapel projecting at the eastern end, begun by Thomas Witney in about 1310, possibly before the chapter house was completed. The [Lady Chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_Chapel "Lady Chapel") seems to have begun as a free-standing structure in the form of an elongated octagon, but the plan changed and it was linked to the eastern end by extension of the choir and construction of a second transept or retrochoir east of the choir, probably by William Joy.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor1967158%E2%80%93164-119)

The Lady Chapel has a vault of complex and somewhat irregular pattern, as the chapel is not symmetrical about both axes. The main ribs are intersected by additional non-supporting, [lierne ribs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lierne_(vault) "Lierne (vault)"), which in this case form a star-shaped pattern at the apex of the vault. It is one of the earliest lierne vaults in England.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor1967158%E2%80%93164-119) There are five large windows, of which four are filled with fragments of medieval glass.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor1967158%E2%80%93164-119) The tracery of the windows is in the style known as Reticulated Gothic, having a pattern of a single repeated shape, in this case a trefoil, giving a "reticulate" or net-like appearance.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor1967158%E2%80%93164-119)

The retrochoir extends across the east end of the choir and into the east transepts. At its centre the vault is supported by a remarkable structure of angled piers. Two of these are placed as to complete the octagonal shape of the Lady Chapel, a solution described by Francis Bond as "an intuition of Genius".[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-120) The piers have attached shafts of marble, and, with the vaults that they support, create a vista of great complexity from every angle.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor1967158%E2%80%93164-119) The windows of the retrochoir are in the Reticulated style like those of the Lady Chapel, but are fully Flowing Decorated in that the tracery mouldings form [ogival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ogive_(architecture) "Ogive (architecture)") curves.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor1967158%E2%80%93164-119)

Eastern end of the cathedral, 1310–45

#### Chapter house

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wells_Cathedral&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Chapter house")]

The [chapter house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapter_house "Chapter house") was begun in the late 13th century and built in two stages, completed about 1310. It is a two-storeyed structure with the main chamber raised on an [undercroft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undercroft "Undercroft"). It is entered from a staircase which divides and turns, one branch leading through the upper storey of [Chain Gate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_Gate,_Wells "Chain Gate, Wells") to Vicars' Close. The [Decorated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_Decorated "Geometric Decorated") interior is described by Alec Clifton-Taylor as "architecturally the most beautiful in England".[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor1967156%E2%80%93158-95) It is octagonal, with its ribbed vault supported on a central column. The column is surrounded by shafts of [Purbeck Marble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purbeck_Marble "Purbeck Marble"), rising to a single continuous rippling foliate capital of stylised oak leaves and acorns, quite different in character from the Early English stiff-leaf foliage. Above the moulding spring 32 ribs of strong profile, giving an effect generally likened to "a great palm tree".[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor1967156%E2%80%93158-95) The windows are large with Geometric Decorated tracery that is beginning to show an elongation of form, and [ogees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ogee "Ogee") in the lesser lights that are characteristic of Flowing Decorated tracery. The tracery lights still contain ancient glass.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor1967156%E2%80%93158-95) Beneath the windows are 51 stalls, the canopies of which are enlivened by carvings including many heads carved in a light-hearted manner.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClifton-Taylor1967156%E2%80%93158-95)
